sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Why am I seeing 503 if this is overload?”
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Why am I seeing 503 if this is overload?”
sections.content:
“Why am I seeing 503 if this is overload?”

Approved response:
“503 is used when the platform is temporarily unable to serve the request due to load shedding or an open circuit breaker. It’s a deliberate, controlled response (with stable error codes) to prevent cascading failures and long tail latency.”

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Approval path (default)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Approval path (default)
sections.content:
Approval path (default)

1) CS/Support compiles incident details and SRE confirmation.
2) SRE provides breach window + summary.
3) Product Dedicated confirms entitlement interpretation (tier/exclusions).
4) Finance (Laura Bennett / delegate) validates policy compliance and amount.
5) Legal (Sofia Mendes / delegate) reviews if there is contract ambiguity or if a non-standard remedy is proposed.
6) CS communicates outcome to customer.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Warm pool / startup considerations
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Warm pool / startup considerations
sections.content:
Warm pool / startup considerations

Some tiers include warm pool guarantees (or faster recovery expectations). During triage, identify if the customer is within a warm-up window:

- Did the deployment recently scale from zero?
- Was there a recent model reload, config change, or node replacement?
- Did traffic resume after prolonged inactivity?

If warm-up is suspected, note it explicitly in the customer thread and ask SRE to confirm whether the event is excluded by policy.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Which tiers are typically credit-eligible?
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Which tiers are typically credit-eligible?
sections.content:
Which tiers are typically credit-eligible?

- **Premium:** written throughput commitment; credit review is standard for confirmed breaches.
- **Plus:** may be eligible depending on contract addenda; treat as “review required.”
- **Standard:** generally best-effort; credit requests require Product + Finance approval.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Is Redwood down?”
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Is Redwood down?”
sections.content:
Common customer questions + approved responses

“Is Redwood down?”

Approved response:
“Not necessarily. These errors indicate Redwood is protecting service reliability during temporary saturation in a specific region/model. We reject early with clear retry guidance to avoid timeouts and degraded performance. Please follow the Retry-After header and exponential backoff. If the issue persists beyond a short window, share correlation IDs and we’ll investigate.”

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > When to initiate a credit review
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > When to initiate a credit review
sections.content:
When to initiate a credit review

Initiate when:

- SRE confirms an SLO breach per canonical evaluator, AND
- The breach is not excluded (e.g., customer throttling), AND
- The customer requests credits OR the account team recommends proactive review.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to interpret and use correlation IDs > Which IDs to ask for
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to interpret and use correlation IDs > Which IDs to ask for
sections.content:
How to interpret and use correlation IDs

Which IDs to ask for

Ask the customer for (in order of preference):
1) `x-redwood-correlation-id` (best for cross-service tracing)
2) `x-redwood-request-id` (single request attempt)
3) Timestamp + region + model + route if IDs are not available

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS)
sections.content:
Triage checklist (Support/CS)

Perform steps 1–8 before (or while) paging; do not block paging for SEV-1.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Golden rules
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Golden rules
sections.content:
Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend)

Golden rules

- **Always respect Retry-After** when provided.
- **Use exponential backoff with jitter**; do not retry immediately.
- **Cap retries** to avoid amplifying overload.
- **Reduce concurrency** rather than increasing it during overload.
- Prefer **idempotency keys** for safe retries on non-streaming requests.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Should I fail over to another model/region?”
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Should I fail over to another model/region?”
sections.content:
“Should I fail over to another model/region?”

Guidance:

- If they have **fallback routing configured** (Dedicated/enterprise Hosted tiers or configured routing policies), yes—recommend they enable/verify it.
- Otherwise, advise them to implement client-side fallback only if they can validate output compatibility and safety.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Appendix: Minimal internal handoff note (for paging)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Appendix: Minimal internal handoff note (for paging)
sections.content:
Appendix: Minimal internal handoff note (for paging)

When paging SRE/Infra, include:

- “Dedicated Throughput SLO: suspected/confirmed”
- Deployment ID
- Tier + region
- Time window and whether ongoing
- Customer-confirmed load/concurrency (if available)
- Dashboard link
- Any correlated symptoms (timeouts, 5xx, queue depth)

This reduces back-and-forth and speeds mitigation.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Common HTTP statuses
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Common HTTP statuses
sections.content:
How to recognize overload-protection responses

Common HTTP statuses

- **429 Too Many Requests**
  - Used for admission controls such as per-tenant concurrency caps, token buckets, or tier limits.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff if Retry-After is provided.

- **503 Service Unavailable**
  - Used when the platform is overloaded at the regional/model level (breaker open) or actively shedding load to protect SLOs.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff and/or reduce load. May persist until capacity recovers.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Customer communications guide > Target update cadence (recommended)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Customer communications guide > Target update cadence (recommended)
sections.content:
Target update cadence (recommended)

- SEV-1: initial response within 15 minutes; updates every 30 minutes until stable.
- SEV-2: initial response within 1 hour; updates every 2–4 hours until stable.
- SEV-3: initial response within 1 business day; updates daily or as material changes occur.

---

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)
sections.content:
When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)

Escalate immediately if any of the following are true:

- **Enterprise customer** reporting sustained overload errors impacting production.
- Overload errors persist for **>15 minutes** with correct backoff behavior.
- **No Retry-After** observed on multiple responses for the same route/region/model.
- Suspected **misclassification** (e.g., 500s that should be 429/503 overload, or overload codes returned with 200/stream interruptions).
- **Fallback routing configured** but not activating.
- Customer reports sharp regression (new errors) coincident with a canary/rollout and provides IDs.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)
sections.content:
Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)

- GPU/node health signals indicate failures, evictions, ECC errors, or repeated container restarts.
- Saturation: GPU utilization pinned while throughput drops (suspected contention, thermal throttling, network bottleneck).
- Capacity: the deployment appears mapped to the wrong pool/shape or lacks the expected headroom.
- Region-wide capacity constraint impacting Dedicated pools.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Post-incident expectations
sections.content:
Post-incident expectations

For confirmed Premium-tier breaches (and significant Plus-tier events), request:

- SRE-written incident summary within 5 business days.
- Follow-up action items tagged to owning teams (SRE/Infra/Observability/Routing).
- If credits were issued: ensure the billing/metering record reflects committed vs burst usage correctly.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Quick triage checklist (Support)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Quick triage checklist (Support)
sections.content:
Quick triage checklist (Support)

1) Confirm this is an overload-protection response (see “How to recognize” below).
2) Verify the customer is following recommended retry/backoff (or advise them to change).
3) Collect required debug info (IDs, time window, region/model, response headers).
4) Determine if this is expected transient overload vs a bug/misconfig (missing Retry-After, incorrect status mapping, fallback not triggering).
5) Escalate to Eng Oncall when criteria are met (see “When to escalate”).

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers
sections.content:
Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers

Use this table to drive consistent customer guidance.

| HTTP | Typical meaning | What Support should say | Customer action |
|------|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| 429 | Admission control / rate limiting / tier cap hit | “Your request was rejected to protect system stability. This is not a model failure; it indicates you are sending requests faster than the current allowed rate/concurrency.” | Respect Retry-After; implement exponential backoff + jitter; reduce concurrency; consider batching; if persistent, discuss tier/capacity options. |
| 503 | Regional/model breaker open or load shedding | “Redwood is temporarily overloaded in the requested region/model. We are rejecting early to avoid timeouts and protect overall reliability.” | Respect Retry-After; backoff + jitter; optionally route to another region/model if configured; reduce max_tokens/streaming concurrency; retry with bounded attempts. |

Notes:

- If the customer reports **timeouts** with no JSON error, treat as a separate issue (possible client/network or upstream timeouts) and escalate based on impact.
- If the customer gets **5xx** without the overload payload, collect details; it may be an unrelated incident.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Templates (copy/paste) > Template C — Request customer confirmation on throttling / load
sections.content:
Template C — Request customer confirmation on throttling / load

Subject: Quick check: request load/concurrency for Dedicated deployment {{deployment_id}}

Hi {{customer_name}},

To confirm whether the deployment is being fully utilized during the impacted window, can you confirm:

- Current concurrency / worker count hitting the deployment
- Whether you have any client-side QPS limits or retries/backoff changes
- Whether the workload mix changed (context length, max output tokens, streaming on/off)

This helps us differentiate capacity/perf issues from under-driven traffic.

Thanks,
{{agent_name}}

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Recommended algorithm (support-approved)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Recommended algorithm (support-approved)
sections.content:
Recommended algorithm (support-approved)

If `Retry-After` is present:

- Sleep `Retry-After` seconds, then retry.

If `Retry-After` is missing:

- Backoff schedule suggestion: 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, then stop (max 4 retries), each with ±20–40% jitter.

Bounds:

- Maximum total retry time budget: **~10–20 seconds** for interactive apps, **~60 seconds** for batch jobs.
- Maximum concurrent retries: keep to a small fraction of steady-state concurrency (e.g., 10–20%).

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.content:
Streaming-specific guidance

Streaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.

- Recommend **lower streaming concurrency** during peak periods.
- If the customer can tolerate it, recommend **shorter outputs** (reduce `max_tokens`) and/or **shorter prompts**.
- If a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.content:
What changed (customer-facing)

When the platform is saturated (GPU capacity, scheduler backlog, downstream dependency brownout), Redwood may reject requests *early* and predictably rather than allowing them to time out or generate random 5xx.

Customers may now see:

- **429** responses for admission / quota / per-tenant caps.
- **503** responses when a regional/model circuit breaker is open or the system is actively shedding load.

These responses:

- Include stable **error codes** and a machine-readable JSON payload.
- Typically include a **Retry-After** header to indicate safe retry timing.
- Include Redwood request/correlation IDs for tracing.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 6) Determine if the issue is isolated or systemic
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 6) Determine if the issue is isolated or systemic
sections.content:
6) Determine if the issue is isolated or systemic

- One deployment vs multiple
- One region vs multiple
- One model family vs multiple

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page SRE On-Call immediately when any of the following is true
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page SRE On-Call immediately when any of the following is true
sections.content:
Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra)

Page SRE On-Call immediately when any of the following is true

- Premium tier customer: reported throughput below committed floor for **>10 minutes**, AND they confirm they are not client-throttled.
- Any tier: a Dedicated Throughput SLO **burn-rate alert** is firing for the deployment.
- Any tier: repeated or escalating customer timeouts/5xx correlated with throughput drop.
- Any tier: throughput drop correlates with recent Redwood changes (rollout, routing, driver/runtime update).

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Internal-only: where to look (for Support with access)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Internal-only: where to look (for Support with access)
sections.content:
Internal-only: where to look (for Support with access)

- Overload dashboards: shed rate, breaker-open rate, queue depth, saturation signals by region/model.
- Incident channels: #eng-oncall, #incidents (look for breaker announcements).
- Runbook: “Hosted overload / circuit breaker runbook” (linked above).

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Severity levels (Support/CS view)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Severity levels (Support/CS view)
sections.content:
Severity levels (Support/CS view)

Use these severities to standardize response; SRE may map to their incident severities.

**SEV-1 (Critical, likely customer-impacting breach)**

- Premium tier customer reports sustained throughput below floor OR SRE burn-rate alert is firing.
- Clear production impact (e.g., queue buildup, timeouts, user-visible latency spikes).
- Immediate paging required.

**SEV-2 (High, likely degradation / at-risk of breach)**

- Throughput is below expected but not yet confirmed as an SLO breach.
- Customer impact is moderate OR limited to a subset of traffic/routes.
- Paging may be required depending on tier and duration.

**SEV-3 (Moderate, investigation / metrics discrepancy)**

- Conflicting metrics (customer vs Redwood dashboards), short-lived dips, or suspected measurement artifacts.
- No clear production impact.

sections.section_path: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.heading: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.content:
- decision_id (stable hash of route_id + tenant_id + evaluation_time + policy_version)
- policy_version
- evaluation_time
- decision_type
- chosen_reason
- target_state (string encoding; owned by controller)
- requested_actions (string encoding; empty in recommend mode)
- evidence (string encoding; ordered)
- annotations (string encoding; includes thresholds, staleness, hold-down state)

Note: In our implementation we’ll likely use structured objects, but for logging/audit we must generate a stable, versioned string representation.

Safety constraints (ADR-043 alignment)

- Anti-flap:
  - Enforce hold-down between flips for non-reachability triggers.
  - Any rollback decision must respect a separate rollback hold-down (avoid ping-pong between primary and fallback).
- Rate limiting:
  - flip_budget_ok must be true, else HOLD.
- Approval hooks:
  - If require_approval is true, decision_type can still be FAILOVER but requested_actions must be empty and “approval_required=true” annotation set.
- Tenant/tier gates:
  - Enterprise/Dedicated can be configured with stricter “do not cross data residency boundary” constraint (policy engine should surface “constraint_violation:data_residency” rather than attempt partial shifts).

Edge cases and expected behavior
1) Partial outage in primary region

- Reachability degraded (not down), 5xx burn elevated, capacity OK in fallback.
- Expected: PARTIAL_SHIFT (e.g., shift 25–50% depending on max_traffic_shift_percent) if corroborated. If sustained and escalates to reachability down or error burn becomes severe => FAILOVER.

2) Signal missing / ingestion delayed

- Any authoritative signal is stale beyond max_staleness_seconds.
- Expected: HOLD. Evidence must explicitly call out staleness and which signal blocked action.

3) Fallback region constrained

- Primary is failing (5xx burn), fallback capacity_hard_gate true.
- Expected: HOLD + annotate “fallback_unhealthy_due_to_capacity”. Controller should invoke load shedding and retry-after rather than shifting load.

4) Control plane degraded

- Control plane health degraded; data plane signals ambiguous.
- Expected: HOLD unless reachability down is authoritative. (Avoid flipping policies when control plane is suspect.)

5) Multi-fallback selection

- If multiple eligible fallback regions are healthy, selection tie-breakers:
  1) policy-specified order
  2) lowest latency probe (if available in inputs)
  3) highest capacity headroom
  4) stable sort by region name

Testing plan (draft)
Unit tests

- Determinism:
  - Same payload with randomized key order => same decision_id, decision_type, evidence ordering.
- Staleness gating:
  - Stale error burn + fresh reachability OK => HOLD.
- Priority:
  - Reachability DOWN overrides hold-down.
  - 5xx burn overrides latency burn when both exceed thresholds.

Integration tests

- Replay recorded signal snapshots from staging incidents + controlled game day traces.
- Validate output is compatible with controller dry-run UX (must contain reasons + evidence).

Performance considerations

- Evaluation must be cheap; do not add per-eval remote calls.
- Evidence strings must be bounded in size. Cap rejected_candidates and evidence list.

Operational / observability hooks

- Emit a single log line per decision with:
  - decision_id, route_id, tenant_id (hashed in shared Hosted contexts), decision_type, chosen_reason
  - key thresholds and freshness
- Export metrics:
  - policy_engine_decisions_total{decision_type, chosen_reason, tier}
  - policy_engine_hold_reasons_total{reason}
  - policy_engine_eval_latency_ms

Open questions

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > General notes
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > General notes
sections.content:
SLOs (targets)

General notes

- SLOs are evaluated over a **rolling 28-day window**.
- Unless specified, targets apply per region (e.g., us-east, eu-west).
- We define both **p95 and p99** latency objectives for enterprise; best-effort uses p95 as primary.

sections.section_path: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.heading: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.content:
- Decision must include:
  - decision_type (NO_OP | FAILOVER | PARTIAL_SHIFT | ROLLBACK | HOLD)
  - chosen_reason (canonical enum)
  - evidence: ordered list of signals used, with values, freshness, and thresholds.
  - rejected_candidates: (optional) top 1–3 alternatives and why they were not selected.

Proposed changes to policy engine
A) New predicates / functions
1) region_health(region, signal_type) -> {status, value, confidence, freshness_seconds}

- Wrapper that pulls normalized data from payload and enforces freshness calculations.

2) is_authoritative_reachability_down(region) -> bool

- True only if:
  - reachability.status == down
  - confidence >= configured_min_confidence (default 0.9)
  - freshness_seconds <= reachability_max_staleness (default 30s)

3) burn_rate_exceeded(region, metric, window, threshold) -> bool

- Works for errors_5xx_burn and tail_latency_burn.
- Window must be one of approved windows (e.g., 1m/5m/30m) to avoid configuration drift.

4) capacity_hard_gate(region) -> bool

- True if headroom below threshold AND capacity signal confidence is high.
- Intended to prevent shifting into an already overloaded region.

5) corroborated(primary_signal, secondary_signal) -> bool

- Enforces ADR-042 “required corroboration signals” when configured.
- Example: if tail latency burn triggers, require either 5xx burn OR reachability degraded/down OR control plane degraded.

6) hold_down_active(last_flip_at, min_hold_down_seconds) -> bool

- If true, policy engine returns HOLD unless reachability down is authoritative.

7) flip_budget_ok(tenant_id, route_id, max_flips_per_hour) -> bool

- Input includes a precomputed counter from controller/state store (policy engine does not store state).

8) blast_radius_ok(tenant_tier, requested_action) -> bool

- Enforces “can’t shift more than X% traffic for tier Y without approval”.
- For Hosted, blast radius is route-scoped; for Dedicated, pool-scoped.

B) Deterministic evaluation mode (required)

- Add an “evaluation_mode” field:
  - recommend: compute decision + evidence; do not mark as executable
  - enforce: compute decision; include explicit requested_action(s)
- Engine must produce identical decision_type and evidence in both modes (action packaging differs).

C) Signal hierarchy evaluation (ADR-042)
Priority order (proposed canonical order for v1):
1) Reachability DOWN (authoritative) => FAILOVER (unless no healthy fallback)
2) Errors (5xx) fast burn (high severity) => FAILOVER or PARTIAL_SHIFT depending on blast radius and capacity
3) Tail latency burn (p99/p95) => PARTIAL_SHIFT first; escalate to FAILOVER if corroborated and sustained
4) Capacity exhaustion / hard gate => HOLD + load shed (controller action), avoid shifting into constrained region
5) Control plane degradation => HOLD (do not flip rapidly; prevent oscillation)

Notes:

- “No healthy fallback” means every eligible fallback region fails capacity_hard_gate OR reachability is down OR stale beyond threshold.
- If no healthy fallback, decision should be HOLD and include “degrade_allowed=true” hint (controller can activate load shedding / retry-after).

D) Policy language / config schema additions
Add new fields (names tentative):

- failover:
  - enabled: boolean
  - eligible_regions: [us-east, eu-west, ...]
  - signal_requirements:
    - primary_trigger: enum
    - corroboration: [enum]
    - min_confidence: float
    - max_staleness_seconds: int
  - dampening:
    - min_hold_down_seconds: int
    - require_sustain_seconds: int (for non-reachability triggers)
  - safety:
    - require_approval: boolean (default true for prod initially)
    - max_flips_per_hour: int
    - max_traffic_shift_percent: int
    - rollback:
      - auto_rollback_enabled: boolean
      - rollback_after_seconds: int
      - rollback_require_healthy_primary_seconds: int

E) Output schema
Decision output (single object, JSON):

sections.content:
Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft

Source type: google_drive
Document ID: dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Draft Spec: Policy Engine Extensions for Regional Failover Automation

Context / why this exists

- We’re upgrading regional failover automation as part of Reliability Program (Q1–Q2 2026). Today, routing policy evaluation has a few gaps:
  - Non-deterministic behavior in edge cases (e.g., multiple signals firing, partial signal availability, time-window ambiguity).
  - Hard to reason about priority across trigger signals (reachability, 5xx burn, tail latency burn, capacity exhaustion).
  - No first-class “hold-down” / dampening in evaluation; logic is split between policy rules and external controller.
  - No consistent mechanism to enforce safety constraints per tenant/tier (max flips, blast radius caps, required approval).

Goals

- Add policy engine primitives so failover decisioning is:
  - Deterministic and auditable (same inputs => same decision; explainability built-in).
  - Compatible with ADR-042 (signal priority + corroboration) and ADR-043 (rollback + anti-flap).
  - Safe by default (rate limits, required corroboration, blast radius constraints).
- Support both:
  - “Recommend” (dry-run) mode: compute candidate flips + evidence.
  - “Enforce” mode: same evaluation but returns executable actions.

Non-goals

- Replace the automation controller. The controller still orchestrates execution, approvals, and cross-system workflow.
- Re-architect signal ingestion. We consume normalized, time-bucketed signals from Region Health + SLO toolkit.
- Build customer-facing UI here.

Terminology

- Policy: configuration describing routing behavior for a route/service/model/tier.
- Region set: primary and fallback regions eligible for this route.
- Trigger signal: normalized boolean or scalar indicating regional impairment or risk.
- Decision: computed outcome (no-op, failover, partial shift, rollback, hold).
- Action: executable change (policy flip, weight adjustment, circuit breaker mode) emitted by controller.

Inputs / data model assumptions

- Policy engine receives inputs as a single evaluation payload, including:
  - route_id (e.g., hosted.chat.completions, dedicated.pool.<pool_id>)
  - tenant_id (optional for shared Hosted; required for Dedicated)
  - tenant_tier (free/pro/enterprise/dedicated)
  - current_routing_state (primary region, weights, last_flip_at)
  - signals (per region, per signal type):
    - reachability: ok|degraded|down + confidence + last_updated
    - errors_5xx_burn: burn_rate + window + confidence
    - tail_latency_burn: burn_rate + p95/p99 deltas + confidence
    - capacity_headroom: percent + “hard gate” boolean
    - control_plane_health (optional): ok|degraded|down
  - evaluation_time (UTC epoch + monotonic sequence)
  - constraints (policy-level + tenant-level): max_flips_per_hour, min_hold_down_seconds, require_approval, blast_radius_limit

Determinism requirements (core)
1) Stable ordering

- Evaluation must not depend on map iteration order.
- Rule matching must define explicit ordering: by priority, then by tie-breakers.

2) Stable time semantics

- All windowed signals must be anchored to evaluation_time and include:
  - effective_start, effective_end, and a “freshness” timestamp.
- Engine must treat stale signals consistently:
  - If authoritative signals are stale beyond threshold, decision = HOLD (do not fail over) unless reachability is explicitly DOWN with high confidence.

3) Single decision per evaluation

- For a given (route_id, tenant_id, evaluation_time), engine emits exactly one decision object, even if multiple actions are possible.
- Multi-step actions (e.g., drain -> shift weights -> finalize) must be represented as a sequence recommendation but still within a single decision record.

4) Explainability

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Overload / throttling semantics
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Overload / throttling semantics
sections.content:
Overload / throttling semantics

Requests may be rejected with HTTP **429** for:

- **Quota/rate limit enforcement** (tenant policy)
- **Overload shedding/admission control** (fleet protection)

We distinguish causes via standardized reason code headers/payloads (see Support doc for exact fields). For SLO accounting, we treat quota-throttled and overload-shed requests differently by tier (see SLI rules below).

sections.section_path: 1769014420 Eu Data Residency Objection Handling
sections.heading: 1769014420 Eu Data Residency Objection Handling
sections.content:
Marcus Lin: approved approach: “We route based on the region selected; cross-region routing of customer content is not the standard behavior for region-pinned setups.” Don’t use “never.” If they require a hard guarantee, push to Dedicated/Private + contract language.

Naomi Feldman: Also don’t conflate “data residency” with “data retention.” They’ll ask “how long do you store prompts/logs in EU.” That’s a separate set of knobs depending on deployment.

Avery Johnson: Can you list the top “DON’T SAY” bullets? Helps AEs avoid stepping on landmines.

Olga Petrov: DON’T SAY / avoid:

- “We guarantee EU-only storage for all data, including logs/metadata” (too broad; depends on category + contract)
- “We never route outside the EU under any circumstances” (absolute)
- “We have ISO 27001 certification” (unless explicitly true; use “alignment” language only if approved)
- “Only EU employees can access your data” (personnel location commitments aren’t part of standard controls)
- “We can meet GDPR/Schrems II by default” (legal conclusion; we can describe controls + DPA)

Olga Petrov: DO SAY:

- “EU region selection / region-pinning for Customer Content processing”
- “Access is least-privilege, audited, and requires authorization”
- “Dedicated/Private options for stricter residency boundaries”
- “We can review specific contractual requirements with Legal/GRC”

Priyom Das: They asked if prompts are used to train models. Can we include that line or keep scoped?

Marcus Lin: You can include the standard line if it comes up, but keep it separate from residency so it doesn’t read like a new promise. Approved phrasing is “We do not use Customer Content to train Redwood-provided models unless the customer explicitly opts in under a separate written agreement.” (Don’t improvise.)

Stephanie Nguyen: For live deal: recommend we send the snippet + link the canonical residency/retention overview in Confluence, and offer a quick security call w/ GRC. @Hannah Schmitt I can help coordinate.

Hannah Schmitt: super helpful. Can someone drop the Confluence link name so I don’t grab the wrong doc?

Daniel Carter: Use the customer-facing page in the Security & Compliance space: “Data retention and deletion overview” (has residency notes). If they want SOC 2 report / evidence, follow the “SOC 2 customer evidence request playbook” and ensure NDA is in place.

Lukas Meyer: :thumbsup: I’ll reuse the snippet for my EMEA deal too.

Hannah Schmitt: Thanks all. I’ll reply to the prospect with the approved paragraph + “we can evaluate stricter residency / contractual needs via Dedicated/Private” and pull Legal/GRC if they push on absolute EU-only + EU-only personnel. :white_check_mark:

Jordan Blake: +1 on escalation. If this is a gating item, loop me in early so we don’t burn cycles. Use the approved wording only—no custom commitments in email.

Hannah Schmitt: ack. looping you + @Stephanie Nguyen on the thread w/ the account notes.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Dashboard requirements (minimum)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Dashboard requirements (minimum)
sections.content:
Dashboard requirements (minimum)

Every protected route must have:

- Availability by tier (enterprise vs best-effort)
- Latency p95/p99 by tier (and TTFB for streaming)
- 429 rate split by reason code (quota vs overload)
- shed_rate and admission_control_active
- queue depth and scheduler lag for backing pools
- Annotations for config changes, feature flag toggles, fallback activation

See the dashboard spec for panel/query naming conventions.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > Latency SLOs by route and tier
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > Latency SLOs by route and tier
sections.content:
Latency SLOs by route and tier

Latency objectives are defined in terms of:

- **Chat streaming:** TTFB p95/p99
- **Non-streaming:** E2E p95/p99

| Route | Tier | Latency SLO (primary) | Latency SLO (secondary) | Measurement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | TTFB p95 ≤ 450ms | TTFB p99 ≤ 900ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Best-effort | TTFB p95 ≤ 900ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1800ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (non-streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 1.8s | E2E p99 ≤ 3.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 350ms | E2E p99 ≤ 800ms | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 700ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 550ms | E2E p99 ≤ 1.2s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 1.2s | (informational) p99 ≤ 2.5s | Gateway E2E |

**Notes / caveats**

- Latency SLOs assume nominal prompt and response sizes. Excessive prompt length or extreme max_tokens increases may be subject to policy limits; those requests are still included in latency metrics unless explicitly rejected by policy.
- Where fallback is permitted (route/model policy), latency SLI measures the actual served path; dashboards must annotate fallback activations.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 2) Latency SLI
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 2) Latency SLI
sections.content:
2) Latency SLI

Latency is measured at the gateway edge (request receive to first byte / completion) and reported as:

- **TTFB (time-to-first-byte)** for streaming endpoints.
- **E2E response time** for non-streaming.

We maintain distinct latency SLO targets per tier and route (see tables below).

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Purpose
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This document defines **per-route SLOs and error budget policy** for Redwood Inference’s **Hosted API** as it relates to **hot-route capacity protection** (tier-aware quotas, priority routing, and controlled shedding).

The intent is to:

- Explicitly define **enterprise vs best-effort** expectations for the highest-traffic routes.
- Make overload behavior **measurable and supportable** (clear SLIs + dashboards + alerts).
- Align alerting to overload protection so we page on **enterprise degradation**, not expected best-effort shedding.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Operational guidance > How to interpret 429s for SLOs
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Operational guidance > How to interpret 429s for SLOs
sections.content:
Operational guidance

How to interpret 429s for SLOs

- **Enterprise 429 overload-shed:** treat as incident-worthy and investigate capacity signals, admission thresholds, route budgets, and pool weights.
- **Best-effort 429 overload-shed:** expected under pressure; use this to validate the protection is working (enterprise should remain stable).
- **Quota 429 (any tier):** not an SLO failure; route to Support/Solutions for policy adjustment if needed.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Protected routes
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Protected routes
sections.content:
Protected routes

Protected routes are selected based on:

- Fleet-wide traffic concentration (hot routes)
- High enterprise SLO/SLA coupling
- Known overload blast radius

Current protected route set:

- `/v1/chat/completions` (includes streaming)
- `/v1/embeddings`
- `/v1/rerank`
- `/v1/completions` (legacy; still used by some enterprise SDKs)

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Route tiers
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Route tiers
sections.content:
Definitions

Route tiers

We classify requests into one of the following tiers at the gateway/policy engine:

- **Enterprise (Protected):** SLA-bearing tenants and allowlisted enterprise accounts for protected routes. These requests receive priority admission and are protected during fleet pressure.
- **Best-effort:** all other traffic. Best-effort may be throttled earlier and more aggressively to preserve fleet health and enterprise budgets.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 1) Availability SLI (server success)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 1) Availability SLI (server success)
sections.content:
1) Availability SLI (server success)

**Definition:** percentage of requests that return an eligible success response.

- Success codes: `2xx` (and `3xx` if any internal redirects apply; typically none)
- Failures: `5xx`, `408`, `499` (client disconnect) are counted as failures unless explicitly excluded by route-specific rules below.

**Tier handling of 429:**

- **Enterprise:** `429` due to *overload shedding/admission control* counts as **unavailable** (because enterprise is protected; overload shed should be rare and indicates under-provisioning or misconfiguration).
- **Best-effort:** `429` due to overload shedding/admission control does **not** count as unavailable (it is expected behavior under pressure). Quota/rate-limit 429s are not counted as availability failures for either tier.

**Note:** 429 classification must be based on the reason code emitted by gateway/policy engine, not inferred from rate.

Alert principles

- Use multi-window burn rate to avoid flapping.

Error budgets

Error budget calculation

For an SLO target **T** over a 28-day window:

- Error budget = **1 − T**

Examples:

- 99.95% availability ⇒ 0.05% error budget (≈ 21.6 minutes of downtime equivalent over 28 days)
- 99.5% availability ⇒ 0.5% error budget

We track budgets separately per:

- route
- region
- tier

sections.content:
Overload protection operational alerts

These are predictive/guardrail alerts. Configure as:

- **Page (Sev2):** enterprise overload shedding sustained
  - enterprise `shed_rate` > **0.1%** for **10 minutes** (any protected route)
- **Ticket:** best-effort shedding unexpectedly high at low utilization
  - best-effort `shed_rate` > **20%** for **15 minutes** AND GPU utilization < **65%** (indicates policy mis-tuning or signal errors)
- **Ticket:** queue depth / scheduler lag sustained without corresponding shedding
  - queue depth > threshold for **10 minutes** with `admission_control_active=false` (indicates missing trigger wiring)

sections.content:
Budget stop-the-line triggers

For enterprise protected routes, any of the following triggers a “stop the line” review in the weekly reliability sync (or async in #eng-sre if urgent):

- Availability error budget burn ≥ **50%** in 7 days
- p99 latency SLO violated for ≥ **2 hours** in a day (sustained)
- Overload shedding observed for enterprise traffic (non-zero sustained) outside planned game day / load test windows

sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Error budget policy (what we do when we burn)
sections.content:
Error budget policy (what we do when we burn)

**Enterprise (Protected) routes**

- If burn is elevated, the default stance is **protect SLOs over throughput**.
- Allowed mitigations (in priority order):
  1) Tighten best-effort admission control thresholds (shed earlier)
  2) Temporarily reduce best-effort burst allowances
  3) Increase enterprise reserved capacity / pool weights (if available)
  4) Enable guarded fallback policies where contractually allowed
  5) As last resort: temporary enterprise throttling with exec/on-call approval and proactive comms

**Best-effort routes**

- Best-effort can be shed under pressure; we do not page purely on best-effort 429 shedding.
- If best-effort availability drops due to 5xx (not 429 overload-shed), we investigate as a normal reliability regression.

sections.content:
Latency SLOs by route and tier

Latency objectives are defined in terms of:

- **Chat streaming:** TTFB p95/p99
- **Non-streaming:** E2E p95/p99

| Route | Tier | Latency SLO (primary) | Latency SLO (secondary) | Measurement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | TTFB p95 ≤ 450ms | TTFB p99 ≤ 900ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Best-effort | TTFB p95 ≤ 900ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1800ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (non-streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 1.8s | E2E p99 ≤ 3.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 350ms | E2E p99 ≤ 800ms | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 700ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 550ms | E2E p99 ≤ 1.2s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 1.2s | (informational) p99 ≤ 2.5s | Gateway E2E |

**Notes / caveats**

- Latency SLOs assume nominal prompt and response sizes. Excessive prompt length or extreme max_tokens increases may be subject to policy limits; those requests are still included in latency metrics unless explicitly rejected by policy.
- Where fallback is permitted (route/model policy), latency SLI measures the actual served path; dashboards must annotate fallback activations.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.content:
Streaming-specific guidance

Streaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.

- Recommend **lower streaming concurrency** during peak periods.
- If the customer can tolerate it, recommend **shorter outputs** (reduce `max_tokens`) and/or **shorter prompts**.
- If a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.

sections.section_path: Sup 18510 Streaming Throughput Metric Mismatch
sections.heading: Sup 18510 Streaming Throughput Metric Mismatch
sections.content:
Sup 18510 Streaming Throughput Metric Mismatch

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_a5a5235d973e421c870e11ceea4887ed
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Streaming throughput metric mismatch (customer dashboard vs Redwood export) — suspected token accounting double-count in streaming

Customer (Vidorama) reports inconsistent throughput numbers for their Dedicated deployment when using streaming responses.

Issue summary

- Vidorama is comparing:
  1) Redwood Console throughput panel (tokens/sec) for their Dedicated deployment, and
  2) Their internal measurement based on streamed tokens (client-side) + Redwood usage export.
- They see Redwood Console tokens/sec ~1.8–2.1x higher than their client-side computed throughput for the same time windows.
- Discrepancy appears only for streaming (non-streaming requests match within ~5–10%).

Impact

- Customer confusion + concern about Dedicated throughput SLO reporting accuracy.
- Potential false positives/negatives in SLO compliance if the canonical throughput metric is inflated for streaming.

Customer-provided details

- Workload: chat completions, streaming enabled (server-sent events).
- Typical request: prompt 1–2k tokens, completion 150–400 tokens, 20–60 concurrent streams.
- Sampling window: 5-min rolling, comparing against their Prometheus counters.

Redwood initial checks (Support)

- Confirmed customer is hitting the correct deployment_id and region (us-east).
- Confirmed they are not mixing model variants in the comparison window (pinned to llama-3.1-70b-instruct; occasional mixtral bursts were excluded by customer).
- Confirmed they are not counting input tokens in their client throughput metric (they only count generated tokens).

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1) Run load test against a Dedicated deployment with streaming enabled.
2) Compare:

   - streaming token counter used by throughput dashboard (server-side), vs
   - sum(completion_tokens) from request final usage events (server-side) and/or reconstructed deltas.

3) Observe that for streaming requests, the dashboard-aligned metric increases faster than final usage totals.

Investigation notes (SRE/Obs)

- Hypothesis A: double-counting streamed completion tokens (both per-chunk deltas and final usage event contribute to the same counter).
- Hypothesis B: retries/resumes on stream reconnects cause duplicated deltas.
- Hypothesis C: mixed attribution labels (route vs deployment) cause aggregation overlap.

Findings

- We can reproduce consistent ~2x inflation when streaming is enabled and client consumes the full stream.
- Root cause identified in telemetry emission path:
  - For streaming responses, we emit per-chunk token deltas (used for near-real-time throughput).
  - At stream termination, a final usage event is emitted.
  - In the current pipeline, the dashboard throughput counter was incremented by BOTH the per-chunk deltas and the final usage event for the same request.
- This does NOT affect billing totals (billing uses finalized usage only). It affects the real-time throughput metric used in dashboards and SLO evaluation.

Workaround (until fix rollout)

- For customer reporting, use finalized completion token metrics (request end) for streaming workloads:
  - completion_tokens_total (finalized) / wall time
- Avoid using real-time streaming throughput panel for contractual/SLO comparisons until patched.

Next actions

sections.heading: Sliced Ingest 429S Dedicated Pool Priority Class Debug Notes
sections.content:
Sliced Ingest 429S Dedicated Pool Priority Class Debug Notes

Source type: google_drive
Document ID: dsid_8ffbd9fe82df457ca67d4fbc9ff1090c
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Sliced ingest 429s on dedicated pool after migration — priority class + burst pool debug notes (Streamly AI)

Context / why this doc exists

- This is a working scratchpad for SRE/Eng while debugging Streamly AI’s sustained 429s during sliced ingest after dedicated pool migration.
- Source ticket: SUP-864999 (customer-support). This doc is meant to be the “newer truth” vs the older ticket narrative since we’ve learned more post-call + after patch testing.

Customer + impact recap (same as ticket, but condensed)

- Customer: Streamly AI (dedicated tier)
- Environment: prod us-west, dedicated pool dp-132-usw
- Traffic mix:
  - Interactive: short chat calls (priority=high)
  - Background: multipart embedding uploads (priority=background/low) with signed URL chunk completion callbacks
- Observed on 2026-03-10 ~09:00–11:30 PDT:
  - ~30% of short chat requests returned 429 coincident with the scheduled bulk ingest flush
  - Customer saw retry amplification and user-visible errors

Versions / components

- Dedicated pool: dp-132-usw
- Ingest coordinator version (at time of incident): 2026.02.3
- Rate-limiter version (at time of incident): 1.14.0-canary
- Edge / API gateway involved due to opaque 429 behavior (missing headers)

Symptoms (what we saw)

- Persistent 429s for /v1/chat during background upload ramp.
- Throttle headers when present indicated per-route window exhaustion.
- A subset of 429s were “opaque” (no X-RateLimit headers) especially during callback fanout peaks.

Example log snippets (from ticket; kept here for reference)

- 2026-03-10T09:02:14Z - 200 - /v1/chat - key=acct-streamly-01 - latency=62ms
- 2026-03-10T09:02:19Z - 429 - /v1/chat - key=acct-streamly-01 - throttle: route_window=0/100
- 2026-03-10T09:02:20Z - 429 - /v1/embed - key=acct-streamly-01 - chunk=12/20 - err=quota_exhausted
- 2026-03-10T09:05:01Z - 429 - /v1/chat - key=acct-streamly-01 - no-rate-headers (opaque)

Steps to reproduce (traffic shape)
1) 100 concurrent short chat requests (avg 50ms) + 20 parallel multipart embedding uploads (avg 45s each).
2) Route both traffic shapes through dp-132-usw with priority classes: interactive=high, background=low.
3) Start background uploads in tight window (cron-style flush ~09:00 local).
4) Observe interactive 429s during the first 20–40 minutes of background ramp.

What changed vs initial hypothesis (updated findings)

- Initial hypothesis in SUP-864999: “priority class mismatch / weight inversion in 1.14.0-canary allows background to borrow interactive burst credits under certain attach sequences.”
- Updated after deeper review (2026-03-13 to 2026-03-20):
  - There are TWO overlapping issues:
    (A) Rate-limiter burst-pool attach race (real) that can temporarily mis-attribute available burst credits across pools.
    (B) Edge proxy early-return path under backpressure causing missing X-RateLimit headers and (worse) collapsing distinct upstream 429 reasons into a single opaque 429 surface.
  - The attach race (A) increases the probability that interactive tokens are temporarily depleted during the exact window when callback fanout is max.
  - The edge behavior (B) makes it look like “random 429s” and prevents the customer from applying correct retry/backoff logic.

Root cause (current best explanation)

Sup 3812 Northwind Dedicated Latency Spike During Interview Window

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_0c504258cd0c432d898e6711fb90eaf6
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Northwind Commerce (Dedicated): transient p95 latency spike during case study measurement/interview window

Issue summary

- Northwind Commerce noticed an elevated p95 latency window on their Dedicated cluster while Marketing/SE were collecting performance numbers for a planned public case study.
- The spike was transient (~18 minutes) but would materially change any "single-window" p95 figure if captured during that interval.

Customer impact

- Endpoint: /v1/chat.completions (streaming + non-streaming)
- Impact: p95 increased from baseline ~430–520ms to ~1.6–2.1s; p99 peaked ~3.8s.
- Error rate: no sustained 5xx increase; brief uptick in 429s due to queue protection (max in-flight).
- User-visible symptoms: slower first-token latency on some requests; a few retries observed by Northwind.

Context (why ticket was opened)

- This was surfaced during case study preparation (interview + metric capture). We need to:
  1) confirm whether the spike was a platform issue vs workload change,
  2) ensure mitigations prevent recurrence during future measurement windows,
  3) document the event so published metrics are measured over an appropriate window (e.g., 7–30 days) and/or exclude known maintenance events.

Timeline (UTC)

- 2025-10-09 16:42: Northwind reports "latency feels off" in Slack via CSM; SE flags risk to published p95.
- 16:46: Support opens SUP-3812; on-call begins triage.
- 16:50–17:08: p95 elevated; queue depth rises; autoscaler events noted.
- 17:10: Tail latency returns to baseline without customer changes.
- 17:35: Initial hypothesis shared with SE/Marketing; agree to avoid quoting that window.

Observability / dashboards

- Dedicated overview (Grafana): https://grafana.redwoodinference.com/d/ded-nw/northwind-dedicated-overview?from=2025-10-09T16:30:00Z&to=2025-10-09T18:00:00Z
- API p95 by route (Datadog): https://app.datadoghq.com/dashboard/3xq-9qk-7eu/northwind-api-latency?from_ts=1760027400000&to_ts=1760032800000
- Scheduler queue depth: https://grafana.redwoodinference.com/d/sched-q/scheduler-queue-depth?var=cluster=northwind-dedicated-us-east
- Node events (maintenance/drain): https://grafana.redwoodinference.com/d/k8s-ev/k8s-events?var=namespace=nw-dedicated

What we checked

- Workload: No evidence of a step-function traffic increase from Northwind; request rate remained within typical burst bounds (+8% vs same weekday baseline).
- Model/version: No model rollout; pinned model version unchanged.
- Platform: K8s events showed a single GPU node drain/replace in the Dedicated pool coincident with the spike.

Investigation notes (most likely cause)

- Root cause: transient capacity reduction during a node drain (kernel security patch) combined with conservative surge settings for the deployment, leading to fewer ready replicas for ~10–15 minutes.
- Contributing factors:
  - Warm-up for the replacement node took longer than expected (image pull + cache warm), increasing request queue depth.
  - Autoscaler reacted, but scale-up lag (GPU provisioning) meant tail latency increased before capacity stabilized.

Mitigation applied

- Short-term (same day):
  - Increased min_replicas for Northwind Dedicated deployment from 6 -> 8 during business hours.
  - Adjusted pod disruption budget to reduce simultaneous unready capacity during drains.
  - Coordinated with Infra to pause non-urgent maintenance on Northwind’s Dedicated pool during the case study measurement week.
- Follow-up hardening:
  - Added an alert on "ready replicas < desired" + queue depth correlation for Dedicated clusters.
  - Documented recommended measurement window guidance for Marketing/SE: use rolling 7-day p95 (excluding maintenance/drain events) or present a range with a footnote.

Customer comms

Incident Bot: :rotating_light: *INCIDENT* (beta) - "rollout split mismatch" reported by Northstar in us-east. Expected canary=10%, observed ~35-45% over last 10m. Route: `hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod`. Rollout: `rlt_7f2c`.

Mina Haddad: on it. This is traffic-splitting enforcement in data plane. If it’s only us-east, could be hash input mismatch on that cluster or a config propagation issue.

- Capacity ask: Reserved pool sized for 8 sustained A100-equivalent GPUs per primary region (NA + EU). Expected steady-state: ~350–600 RPS for short payload chat (avg token window 256). Burst to ~1k RPS during shift changes.
- Performance targets: P95 text-gen latency <= 80ms, P99 <= 220ms for chat on dedicated pool; throughput guarantees of 500 RPS sustained per region.
- SLA position (customer asks): 99.95% uptime across dedicated pools; 30% credit at 99.9–99.95; 50% credit below 99.9; request for monthly credit cap and cumulative measurement window.
- Redwood counterproposals discussed: baseline 99.95 SLA with quarterly reconciliation; credit schedule tiered: 99.9–99.95 = 10% service credit, 99.5–99.9 = 30%, <99.5 = 60% (proposal to legal). Redwood wants max cap at 6 months' fee.

sections.content:
B) Traffic split mismatch

**Common symptoms:**

- Observed canary traffic differs significantly from configured percent.
- Split matches overall, but **per-region** mismatch (e.g., us-east OK, eu-west off).
- Mismatch only for streaming requests or retries.
- Canary sees 0% traffic despite non-zero configuration.

**Likely causes:**

- Deterministic cohort key mismatch (unexpected hashing input due to missing user/session key).
- Sticky assignment changes across retries (incorrect retry key usage).
- Multi-region propagation lag (config not yet applied everywhere).
- Data plane caching old route config.
- A/B test or fallback routing policy taking precedence (policy evaluation order).

Int 9821 Crucible Inference Latency Spike And 5Xx Inc 9821

Source type: jira

Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Crucible Health: inference latency spike + transient 5xx on /v1/generate (INC-9821)

Customer escalation relayed by Stephanie Nguyen. Crucible Health reported sudden latency spike and burst of 5xx on inference endpoint /v1/generate beginning ~2026-08-28 07:55 PDT. Reported impact: median latency increased from ~120ms to ~900ms; throughput dropped from ~250 req/s to ~150 req/s for Crucible production key; initial customer-observed 5xx rate ~8% during the window; multiple batches timed out and downstream throttles triggered. Customer had a critical demo at 10:00 PDT.

Immediate hypotheses (serving): autoscaler oscillation under burst + degraded single shard causing head-of-line blocking.

Immediate mitigations executed: emergency scale-up of dedicated pool (target +20% capacity) + temporary concurrency limit increase + drain suspected bad instance(s) + enable routing of new requests to compatible fallback model variant (lower context) to reduce per-token work.

Outcome (updated after investigation): improvements observed within ~9–12 minutes; throughput returned to baseline and tail latency normalized after draining the degraded node(s) and reverting autoscaler policy.

Updated root cause (post-incident): the triggering event was an autoscaler policy update that reduced stabilization/cooldown and interacted poorly with a burst in queue depth, causing scale oscillation. One GPU instance concurrently entered a degraded driver state (intermittent kernel launch stalls rather than a hard OOM), amplifying tail latency and increasing request timeouts which surfaced as 5xx at the gateway. The instance replacement lag plus oscillation extended the incident duration.

sections.content:
Page 4: Evaluation best practices

**Proposed title:** “How to evaluate quality and latency before rollout”

**Customer-friendly guidance**

- Suggested evaluation approach:
  - Identify representative prompts (production samples + edge cases).
  - Run baseline vs profile-enabled comparisons.
  - Use A/B sampling (e.g., 1–5% traffic) with a rollback threshold.

- What to measure
  - Quality: task-specific metrics (pass@k, exact match, ranking metrics) + human review where appropriate.
  - Latency: p50/p95 decode latency and time-to-first-token.
  - Cost: cost/token and throughput.

- Rollout strategy
  1) Enable in staging on a non-critical route
  2) Canary in production (small % traffic)
  3) Expand gradually with monitoring

- Provide explicit “stop conditions”
  - Elevated fallback rate
  - Increased error rate
  - Statistically meaningful quality regression on a defined slice

**Note:** We cannot publish Redwood’s internal thresholds verbatim if they are considered sensitive, but we can publish recommended guardrails (e.g., “predefine acceptable deltas and require sign-off”). We will align with Selene Huang (quality guardrails) on what’s safe to disclose.

Go-Live Protocols: Cross-Org Communications & Escalation
Summary
-------
This document defines the cross-organizational go-live protocol used by Redwood Inference for enterprise tenant cutovers. It focuses on communications, stakeholder coordination, and an escalation ladder tailored for high-risk or high-visibility customers. Use this runbook as the canonical checklist for the 72 hours before, during, and 72 hours after a cutover where multiple teams (Customer Success, SRE, Solutions Engineering, Product, and Sales) must be coordinated.

Scope
-----

- Applies to: Dedicated and Private deployment go-lives and tenant migrations with SLA commitments (any customer with an enterprise contract or > $50k monthly spend).
- Out of scope: self-serve trial accounts, routine model-only updates without routing changes.

Goals and SLOs to Protect
-------------------------

- Availability SLA target to protect during cutover: 99.9% (monthly) for production routes.
- Immediate remediation thresholds (trigger escalation):
  - Error rate spike: sustained >5% errors for 5 minutes across tenant endpoints.
  - Latency spike: P95 latency >2000ms for 10 minutes.
  - Token cost anomaly: >200% of projected token spend in 30 minutes.
  - KV cache miss-rate >30% sustained for 15 minutes (for cache-sensitive workloads).

Pre-Cutover (T-72 to T-1 hours)
-------------------------------

1. Confirm stakeholders and channels
   - Primary CSM (Customer Success Manager): name + mobile number.
   - Tech lead (Customer): contact + escalation path.
   - Solution Engineer (SE): responsible for ingress, API contract verification.
   - Oncall SRE/Platform owner: PagerDuty schedule and runbook owner.
   - Slack channels: #cs-<customer>-go-live (private channel), #oncall-redwood, #se-ops.
2. Telemetry sanity checks — must pass before proceeding:
   - Synthetic journey (happy path) passes end-to-end: <customer> -> Redwood API -> response < 1s.
   - PromQL checks: error_rate/instance < 0.005 for 10m; p95_latency_query < 1500ms.
3. Canary plan and acceptance criteria
   - Canary traffic: route 1% of production for 30 minutes with zero critical errors.
   - Acceptance: no P0/P1 incidents during canary and no regression in model quality metrics (if applicable).
4. Whitelist and firewall confirmations
   - Verify ingress IP ranges, customer egress rules, and TLS client certs.

During Cutover (T0 to +4 hours) — Immediate Checklist
----------------------------------------------------

- Primary communications protocol:
  - All updates posted to #cs-<customer>-go-live every 10 minutes during the first hour, then every 30 minutes until stable.
  - The CSM posts customer-facing status updates; technical details posted to private channel only.
- Live monitoring dashboard (owner: Oncall SRE):
  - Tenant-specific dashboard showing throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, KV cache hits, token consumption.
- Escalation triggers (first responder must escalate within 5 minutes if triggered):
  1) P0: service unavailable for customer routes — immediate page to P1 oncall and notify Engineering Director.
  2) P1: sustained SLO breach (see thresholds above) — page SE and PM, start RCA and mitigation steps.
  3) P2: model quality regression detected — notify Applied ML and SE; consider traffic switch to verified model snapshot.

Escalation Ladder (contact order and responsibilities)
----------------------------------------------------

Pr 19422 Fix Throughput Metric Double Counting Streaming

Source type: github
Document ID: dsid_4b2ac6984bdf4737a18520e158b04453
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Fix throughput metric double-counting for streaming responses

Problem: Dedicated throughput SLO reporting was overcounting tokens for streaming requests. We were incrementing `deployment_tokens_generated_total` per-stream chunk (delta tokens) and then incrementing again on stream completion using the final `usage.completion_tokens` value. For non-streaming, the completion-path increment is correct; for streaming, it results in ~2x token totals (shape/model dependent) and skews derived tokens/sec in the SLO evaluator + dashboards.

Customer/ops impact: This primarily affects Dedicated throughput SLO compliance tracking (tokens/sec floor) and internal saturation indicators. It also contributed to customer confusion when comparing Console throughput graphs vs request-level `usage` totals (see SUP-18510). Billing exports are not impacted (billing uses metering events, not the SLO throughput counters).

Fix: Make streaming accounting single-source-of-truth by only emitting token increments from the streaming path, and skipping the completion-path increment when `streaming=true`. Additionally, guard against duplicate “final chunk” emission by tracking `last_emitted_completion_tokens` on the stream session and only emitting positive deltas.

What changed: - `api-gateway`: adjust token accounting so the completion handler does not increment throughput counters for streaming requests; the counter is incremented only via the stream chunk emitter. - `telemetry`: add explicit `streaming` + `accounting_source` labels to aid debugging (chunk vs completion). - tests: add unit tests for streaming lifecycle (N chunks + final usage) asserting exact token totals; add regression test covering the previously failing scenario where both chunk deltas and final usage were emitted.

Rollout notes: This changes the magnitude of streaming throughput counters immediately on deploy (expected ~-50% for affected traffic). SRE/Obs have been pinged to annotate the Dedicated throughput SLO dashboard and ignore pre/post comparisons for 24h.

Follow-ups (not in this PR): 1) Backfill/annotation for SLO reports that span the deploy window (SRE to decide). 2) Consider moving all throughput SLO computations to request-level usage events once metering latency is acceptable.

4) Open action items from last week (owners + ETA).
5) Escalations and customer-impacting items.
GO/NO-GO CHECKLIST (my shorthand)

- Safety: latest canary passed golden prompt set? [yes/no] — if no -> NO-GO and block rollout. Owner: Priya.
- Latency: 95th <= SLO (hosted) and Dedicated 90th within committed window? [ok/warn/fail] Owner: Jordan.
- Throughput: capacity test at target qps for model variant (rwx-v2-quant) >= 90% predicted. Owner: Marco (perf eng).
- Telemetry: traces + logs flowing to observability (no gaps > 5 min). Owner: Observability on-call.
- Rollback plan: image rollback verified in staging (time-to-recover < 10m). Owner: me (Aisha) — pre-check: rehearse command set.

LIVE-RUN CUES (during shiproom)

- If latency alert fires: call out metric, ask SRE to confirm impact (hosted vs dedicated). If impact is hosted only -> consider global throttles, otherwise trigger capacity burst.
- If canary fails: pause rollout, gather failing prompts, escalate to Applied ML for quality triage. Capture failing prompt examples in the meeting notes.
- If control plane flaps: deploy cross-region fallback policy, set communication to CS + site-status.

SMOKE-TEST QUICK-LOOK (ordered)
1) /health (all regions) — expect 200 and healthy=true.
2) golden prompt generation (3 variants) — check for coherent output and stable token length.
3) streaming socket smoke (5 simulated clients) — no connection resets.
4) KV cache hit-rate sanity check (> 30% for typical workloads).
5) auth flow: token validation for dev key and prod key.
RISKS I CARE ABOUT (notes to self)

- Quantized model edge cases: hallucinations on long-context prompts unseen in evals. Watch for uptick in hallucination rate on live eval monitors.
- Autoscale cold starts: small percentage of cold starts can push P95 over threshold. Keep warmup policy on for first 2h post-deploy.
- Third-party infra patch windows (cloud provider) could impact Dedicated zones — pre-check weekly maintenance calendar.

OPEN ACTIONS (make sure to call out in meeting)
