sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Open Questions (tracked outside ADR)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Open Questions (tracked outside ADR)
sections.content:
Open Questions (tracked outside ADR)

- Whether to introduce a scheduler_profile tag in baseline keys (cardinality vs attribution benefit).
- Whether to page on runtime-only p95 for certain enterprise-dedicated pools (when E2E has additional network variance).
- Whether to incorporate a lightweight statistical test (e.g., bootstrap CI on p95) for models with unusually high variance.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Minimum samples (per key K, per window)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Minimum samples (per key K, per window)
sections.content:
Minimum samples (per key K, per window)

- **Latency metrics**: minimum **200 successful canary requests** per window.
- **Tokens/sec**: minimum **200 successful canary requests** per window AND minimum **50,000 total generated tokens** per window.

If sample requirements are not met:

- No alert state change is allowed (prevents flapping in low-coverage periods).
- Dashboard panels display “insufficient sample” annotation.

Rationale:

- Tail latency (p95/p99) is unreliable with very small N.
- Tokens/sec needs sufficient token volume to smooth per-request variance.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Positive
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Positive
sections.content:
Consequences

Positive

- Stable, versioned baselines support rollout gates and high-confidence paging.
- Rolling health baseline provides drift visibility without undermining safety.
- Anti-flap controls reduce alert noise and prevent incident-bot storms.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Approval path (default)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Approval path (default)
sections.content:
Approval path (default)

1) CS/Support compiles incident details and SRE confirmation.
2) SRE provides breach window + summary.
3) Product Dedicated confirms entitlement interpretation (tier/exclusions).
4) Finance (Laura Bennett / delegate) validates policy compliance and amount.
5) Legal (Sofia Mendes / delegate) reviews if there is contract ambiguity or if a non-standard remedy is proposed.
6) CS communicates outcome to customer.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > F. Retries and idempotency
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > F. Retries and idempotency
sections.content:
F. Retries and idempotency

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Customer is responsible for implementing idempotency keys for retryable requests. Redwood will use commercially reasonable efforts to avoid duplicate billing for server-side retries performed under the same logical request identifier. Customer-submitted duplicate requests may be billable.”

**Negotiation notes:**

- Do not guarantee “no double billing ever.” Instead: “commercially reasonable efforts” + dispute process.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Exclusions (non-counted windows/requests) > Request-level exclusions
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Exclusions (non-counted windows/requests) > Request-level exclusions
sections.content:
Request-level exclusions

The following requests are excluded from both numerator and denominator:

- **Customer-side throttling or pacing** that prevents the deployment from being demand-saturated while measuring throughput (e.g., the customer sends traffic well below the committed floor and attempts to interpret low throughput as non-compliance).
- **Client disconnects / cancellations** before generation completes (where Redwood terminates work early).
- **Invalid requests** or requests that violate documented limits (e.g., context > supported max for the purchased shape, unsupported model version).
- **Customer-enforced caps** that materially reduce achievable throughput, including:
  - Very low `max_tokens` combined with high request overhead patterns (evaluated case-by-case; see “edge-case review” below)
  - Customer-set concurrency limits below recommended saturation settings

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language)
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language)
sections.content:
Clause library (approved language)

Use the below clauses as starting points. Do not materially alter without Legal review.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Which tiers are typically credit-eligible?
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Which tiers are typically credit-eligible?
sections.content:
Which tiers are typically credit-eligible?

- **Premium:** written throughput commitment; credit review is standard for confirmed breaches.
- **Plus:** may be eligible depending on contract addenda; treat as “review required.”
- **Standard:** generally best-effort; credit requests require Product + Finance approval.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition > Threshold levels
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition > Threshold levels
sections.content:
Threshold levels

Two alert levels exist:

- **Warning**: actionable signal for runtime team triage; routed to #eng-runtime.
- **Paging**: sustained, high-confidence regression on top models; routed to on-call rotation.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Changelog
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Changelog
sections.content:
Changelog

- 2026-02-12: Clarified cooldown timers, added telemetry delay protection rule, and tightened tokens/sec minimum token count requirement.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 5) “Retry”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 5) “Retry”
sections.content:
5) “Retry”

Retry can occur on:

- **Client side** (customer’s SDK/app retries)
- **Server side** (Redwood retries/fallback routing to preserve availability)

Internal positions:

- We aim to bill **once per logical request** where retries are transparently handled under the same idempotency key.
- If the customer does not use idempotency keys and submits duplicate requests, those may be billable.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Observed throughput calculation (tokens/sec)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Observed throughput calculation (tokens/sec)
sections.content:
Observed throughput calculation (tokens/sec)

For each deployment and 5-minute window:

- `observed_tps = eligible_output_tokens / eligible_generation_wall_time_seconds`

Where:

- **eligible_output_tokens** counts output tokens generated for eligible requests whose generation occurs within the window.
- **eligible_generation_wall_time_seconds** is the sum of per-request generation durations for eligible requests, measured at Redwood’s gateway/runtime boundary.

Notes:

- We use **wall time spent generating** rather than total window duration to avoid penalizing low-utilization periods.
- This SLO measures our ability to serve when the customer is asking for capacity, not whether the customer sends enough traffic to saturate the deployment.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Operational playbook links
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Operational playbook links
sections.content:
Operational playbook links

- Escalation and customer comms: confluence://customer-success-and-support/escalation-playbook/dedicated-throughput-slo-escalation
- Tier-aware overload protection: confluence://eng-platform/runbooks/tier-aware-routing-and-overload-protection
- Dedicated throughput dashboards: confluence://eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/dedicated-throughput-slo-dashboards

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Redlines: common asks and recommended responses > 2) “Do not charge for retries / failed requests.”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Redlines: common asks and recommended responses > 2) “Do not charge for retries / failed requests.”
sections.content:
2) “Do not charge for retries / failed requests.”

**Position:** If compute is performed, some usage may be reported.
**Response:** Use idempotency + commercially reasonable efforts clause. Offer a credits mechanism for verified platform-caused duplicate charges.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Rollout Guidance
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Rollout Guidance
sections.content:
Rollout Guidance

- Phase 1 (single region): warnings only, tune per-model overrides until noise is acceptable.
- Phase 2: enable paging only for top models with proven low variance and stable baselines.
- Phase 3: integrate gating with release engineering once paging signal is trusted (warning can gate early as “soft fail,” paging as “hard fail”).

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > C) Per-region baselines always on
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > C) Per-region baselines always on
sections.content:
C) Per-region baselines always on

Pros:

- Reduces false positives due to cross-region fleet differences.

Cons:

- Baseline explosion (more artifacts and config), operational overhead.

Decision: Region is optional and only enabled for models/regions where observed variance requires it.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)
sections.content:
Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)

These are emitted to dashboards and included in alert payloads, but do not page unless explicitly enabled for a model:

- Queueing time p95 +25% (suggests scheduler/fleet saturation)
- Prefill p95 +15% (suggests kernel/model config regressions)
- Decode p95 +15% (suggests kernel/model config regressions)

Rationale:

- Paging should be driven by end-to-end customer-impact proxy (E2E p95 and tokens/sec).
- Breakdown metrics improve triage but are often noisier and more sensitive to load mix.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > G. Measurement system and authoritative records
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > G. Measurement system and authoritative records
sections.content:
G. Measurement system and authoritative records

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Fees are based on Redwood’s measurement systems and usage records. Redwood will provide usage reporting via invoice detail, Console, or usage export/API. In the event of conflict, the invoice and supporting usage report for the billing period will control, subject to Customer’s dispute rights.”

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Redlines: common asks and recommended responses > 3) “Caching must always reduce price.”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Redlines: common asks and recommended responses > 3) “Caching must always reduce price.”
sections.content:
3) “Caching must always reduce price.”

**Position:** Caching may reduce billed tokens depending on eligibility and product policy.
**Response:** Use caching clause; avoid hard commitments. If needed for the deal, define a limited-term promotional adjustment with Finance sign-off.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 2) “Request”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 2) “Request”
sections.content:
2) “Request”

A **Request** is an API call that is accepted by Redwood’s service and results in an attempt to process the call (including streaming requests). Do not tie “request” to “successful response” unless Product/Finance explicitly approves.

sections.section_path: 20260828 Crucible Inference Sitrep
sections.heading: 20260828 Crucible Inference Sitrep
sections.content:
Root cause: A recently deployed autoscaler policy update combined with a rare kernel failure on a single GPU instance produced cascading queue pressure; autoscaler oscillation and a lag in instance replacement led to transient 5xxs and reduced throughput. The failing instance also intermittently returned degraded kernel performance which amplified tail latency.

What we did:

- Emergency capacity bump and routing to fallback model variant on 2026-08-28 at 08:28 PDT — immediate tail-latency improved and throughput returned to baseline within ~12 minutes.
- Drained and reprovisioned the failing instance; patched the kernel path in the affected image and rolled a hotfix to prevent identical failures.
- Reverted the autoscaler policy update and introduced a short cool-down to prevent oscillation.

Impact:

- Customer observed peak 5xx rate of 8% and throughput drop to ~60% of baseline for a ~10-minute window. No customer data exfiltration.

Next steps / action items: 
1) We will publish a short postmortem to the customer by EOD with the timeline and mitigations (Hannah + Stephanie).
2) Engineering (Marcus) to harden autoscaler policy testing and add a canary step for autoscaler changes.
3) Product to add a routing knob for immediate cross-model fallback triggered by SLA breach (Marcus + Product).
4) Finance to confirm priority-burst billing terms for this incident (Laura).

Attachments: postmortem-draft.md, kpi_before_after.png

Thanks everyone for the quick triage. Julia — we are sending a tailored postmortem and are happy to run a joint technical review next week if you'd like.

— Marcus Lin
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime
marcus_lin@redwood.com

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)
sections.content:
B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)

Pros:

- Extremely stable; easy to reason about.

Cons:

- Becomes stale as fleet/hardware/driver changes accumulate; increases false positives over time.
- Forces frequent manual work to remain relevant.

Decision: Rejected as the only strategy. Adopted as primary baseline with explicit regeneration workflows.

When to initiate a credit review

Initiate when:

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > D. Tool/function calling and structured output
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > D. Tool/function calling and structured output

D. Tool/function calling and structured output

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Where the service supports tool/function calling or structured output, tokens attributable to tool call inputs/outputs and associated formatting may be included in token usage as reported by Redwood.”

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > A. Usage unit (Tokens) — baseline clause
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > A. Usage unit (Tokens) — baseline clause
sections.content:
A. Usage unit (Tokens) — baseline clause

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Usage is measured in tokens processed by the applicable model. A token is a unit of text determined by the model’s tokenization scheme. Fees are calculated based on the number of billed tokens reported by Redwood for the applicable billing period. Token counts may vary by model and model version.”

**Negotiation notes:**

- If customer requests a fixed tokenization algorithm, respond that tokenization is model-dependent and tied to the model provider’s implementation.
- If customer requests billing purely on input+output tokens, steer to “billed tokens” and point to reporting transparency.

B. Usage unit (Requests) — when included

sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 3) “Usage Report” / “Usage API”

3) “Usage Report” / “Usage API”

**Usage Report** means Redwood’s reported usage as displayed in the Console, invoice detail, or usage export/API. Contract language should clarify which report is authoritative for billing.

Internal preference:

- For contracts: define that **Redwood’s invoice and supporting usage report** is the authoritative basis for fees, subject to the dispute process.

Internal operational guardrails (contracting)

Month-end close and late-arriving events

- Contract language should not obligate real-time corrections for late events.
- Use the dispute clause and reconciliation process to handle exceptions.

8) Open an incident record (internal) if SEV-1/SEV-2

sections.section_path: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > What happened (symptoms)
sections.heading: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > What happened (symptoms)
sections.content:
What happened (symptoms)

The canary’s regression evaluator compared observed p95 latency/tokens-sec against per-model baselines. After model expansion:

- Many evaluations used **fallback baseline values** because the baseline lookup key did not match (baseline existed under a different dimension set).
- Metric series were fragmented by high-cardinality labels; the regression evaluator saw many “small-N” series and oscillated between “enough samples” and “not enough samples” depending on which series was queried.
- Alert rules did not consistently enforce **minimum sample size across the same grouping** used by the evaluator, which allowed small, noisy slices to trip thresholds.
- incident-bot dedupe keys lacked stable identifiers for (model, version, region, sku, runtime_build), so the same underlying symptom created repeated threads/pages.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Context
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Context
sections.content:
Context

Redwood Inference’s Hosted API sees bursty and highly variable traffic (prompt length variance, streaming concurrency spikes, regional capacity dips). During overload, failures can cascade into:

- Tail-latency blowups (p95/p99), then timeouts
- Elevated 5xx from upstream retry storms and downstream saturation
- Noisy-neighbor effects across tenants and tiers
- Confusing customer experience (timeouts and generic 5xx instead of stable semantics)

We need a layered admission control strategy that:
1) Rejects or degrades traffic early and predictably.
2) Preserves tenant isolation and tier-aware behavior.
3) Avoids feedback loops (e.g., shedding causing routing thrash, or routing failover amplifying load elsewhere).
4) Produces consistent customer-facing overload errors (see ADR-014).

This ADR defines **where circuit breakers and load shedding “live”** across the request path (Gateway → Routing → Runtime) and how signals flow.

sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Why am I seeing 503 if this is overload?”
sections.content:
“Why am I seeing 503 if this is overload?”

Approved response:
“503 is used when the platform is temporarily unable to serve the request due to load shedding or an open circuit breaker. It’s a deliberate, controlled response (with stable error codes) to prevent cascading failures and long tail latency.”

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Implementation notes (non-normative)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Implementation notes (non-normative)
sections.content:
Implementation notes (non-normative)

- Gateway admission should use a combination of:
  - token bucket (QPS) per tenant/route
  - concurrency caps for streaming endpoints
  - “regional overload state” multiplier for dynamic throttling (with hysteresis)
- Runtime should expose clear “reject reasons” that map into ADR-014 overload codes without leaking internals.
- Routing should mark fallback attempts and enforce max_attempts=1. Any further attempt must be a client retry honoring Retry-After.

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
- Total burst attempts: dominated by 2 tenants with scheduled batch jobs.
- Denial rate: ranged 0–18% by tenant depending on time-of-day; spikes correlated with telemetry lag and cooldown behavior.
- Admission controller p99: stable in us-east; spiky in eu-west (timeouts).
- Neighbor impact: one validated event (SUP-28455) where non-burst p99 regressed ~12–18% for ~20 minutes before mitigation.
- Billing reconciliation: identified retry double-counting bug; now fixed but we need ongoing automated checks.

What we changed during beta (already merged or in progress)

- Telemetry smoothing / prevent starvation under lag: GitHub:redwood/pr-23944
- Global circuit breaker for burst pools: GitHub:redwood/pr-23919
- SLO-based auto-gating (reduce/disable burst on non-burst regression): GitHub:redwood/pr-23988
- Billing idempotency + prevent double-counting: GitHub:redwood/pr-24108

GA readiness action items (must do)
P0 (blockers)
1) Telemetry freshness as a first-class signal

- Add metric + alert: “telemetry freshness seconds” by region/hardware + admission controller decision mode (fresh vs degraded).
- In degraded mode: enforce safer decisions (lower caps) + include explicit denial reason “TELEMETRY_STALE_DEGRADED_MODE”.
- Owner: Allison Grant + Logan Wright
- Target: by 2025-06-07

2) EU-West admission controller latency hardening

- Bound dependency calls with strict timeouts; add cached snapshots; add load shedding in controller.
- Define routing behavior when controller is slow: deterministic fallback decision + do not hammer controller.
- Owner: Jordan Lee + Mina Haddad
- Target: by 2025-06-10

3) Retry guidance + “Retry-After” semantics tied to reason codes

- Update docs + support macros.
- Owner: Peter Holtz + Kira Thompson

4) Billing reconciliation automation

- Nightly job: compare metering export vs dashboard aggregates within tolerance; page billing on drift > X%.
- Owner: Nadia Rahman + Cole Summers
- Target: by 2025-06-12

P1 (strongly recommended for GA)
5) Cooldown redesign proposal

- Experiment with sustained-threshold cooldown vs proportional cooldown.
- Add simulation + real-world replay tests.
- Owner: Keiko Yamamoto
- Target: proposal by 2025-06-14; implement behind flag if time.

6) Neighbor impact circuit breaker thresholds

- Define concrete thresholds: p95 delta, tail amplification, and error rate deltas for non-burst tenants.
- Ensure breaker annotations show “why” and which tenant(s) triggered.
- Owner: Sean Gallagher
- Target: 2025-06-14

7) Priority tier fairness tests

- Extend multi-tenant integration tests to include tier mixes; assert starvation bounds.
- Owner: Jordan Lee
- Target: 2025-06-15

8) Console/config propagation SLO + fix

- Set expectation: config changes visible within N minutes; instrument end-to-end propagation time.
- Owner: Chloe Martin

  - Check global circuit breaker status
  - Check telemetry freshness + telemetry lag panels
  - Check admit/deny by reason code
  - Check pool saturation + queue depth

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
Burst Capacity Retro Notes

Source type: google_drive
Document ID: dsid_95c7aa5238f94570a8e0a8684736b666
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Dedicated Burst Capacity — Post-beta retro notes (SRE)
Doc goal
Capture what we learned from the Dedicated Burst Capacity beta (May 2025): what broke, which guardrails were too strict/too lax, what we changed during beta, and what must be completed before GA.

Retro logistics

- Date: 2025-05-28 (60 min)
- Facilitator: Rafael Mendes (SRE)
- Notetaker: Peter Holtz (Routing SRE)
- Beta window covered: 2025-05-06 to 2025-05-24
- Scope: burst pools (regional/hardware), admission controller, routing integration, SLO gates, dashboards/alerts, metering/billing hooks, supportability

Attendees (high signal contributors)

- SRE/Obs: Sean G., Rafael M., Peter H., Allison G., Sergio C.
- Infra/Fleet: Vanessa O., Keiko Y.
- Control plane/policy: Jordan L.
- Routing: Mina H.
- Billing/metering: Cole S., Nadia R.
- CS feedback: Rachel K.

What went well (keep)
1) Global safety cap + circuit breaker concept worked in practice

- We hit the cap once in staging and once “near miss” in prod beta; breaker prevented runaway neighbor impact.
- The playbook of “reduce caps -> drain queues -> disable burst for lowest tiers first” is operationally sound.

2) Denial reason codes improved triage materially

- Support/CS could distinguish “cap reached” vs “pool saturated” vs “cooldown” vs “telemetry stale”.
- Routing logs + reason codes made it clear where to look first.

3) Dashboards were mostly the right primitives

- Saturation, queue depth, admit/deny rates, and p95 deltas by tenant were enough to debug 80% of issues.
- SLO gate signal (non-burst tenant latency regression) is a good north star even if thresholds need tuning.

4) Rollout gating/feature flags prevented blast radius

- Per-region allow list + per-tenant enablement meant we could pause EU-West issues without impacting US-East.

What broke / painful incidents
A) Telemetry lag caused unfair denials + occasional starvation

- Symptom: a few tenants saw denial spikes while pool appeared underutilized; the “laggy” telemetry made the controller think they were still consuming burst tokens.
- Customer-visible effect: burst requests denied unexpectedly; some clients retried aggressively and amplified load.
- Root cause (likely): our admission controller relied on near-real-time usage signals; when signals were delayed, the smoothing window + token bucket refill behavior effectively penalized active tenants.
- Fix during beta: hotfix added smoothing + guard conditions + conservative fallback when telemetry freshness is below threshold.
- Ref: GitHub:redwood/pr-23944

B) EU-West burst admission timeouts (controller dependency chain)

- Symptom: admission calls intermittently timed out in eu-west under high request rate; routing fell back but increased gateway error rates briefly.
- Root cause: admission controller p99 latency spiked due to dependency (policy evaluation + fleet telemetry query) not being bounded; threadpool saturation.
- Mitigation: enable circuit breaker + temporarily tighten per-tenant caps + disable burst in eu-west allow list until patched.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28579

C) Billing: burst usage double-counted on retry paths

sections.section_path: Sup 3812 Northwind Dedicated Latency Spike During Interview Window
sections.heading: Sup 3812 Northwind Dedicated Latency Spike During Interview Window
sections.content:
- We informed Northwind that we identified a transient capacity event (node drain) and applied safeguards to reduce the chance of recurrence. No action required on their side.

Resolution

- Latency returned to baseline at 2025-10-09 17:10 UTC.
- Preventative changes are in place (min replicas + PDB + maintenance pause).
- Guidance provided to Marketing/SE to avoid quoting p95 captured during the impacted interval; use an agreed measurement window for publication.

Next steps / action items
1) Infra: validate node warm-up time on Dedicated pools; ensure image pre-pull + model cache warm path for replacement nodes (linked PR: redwood-inference/infra#19344).
2) Runtime: add "pre-warm" hook to reduce first-request penalty after replica replacement (linked PR: redwood-runtime#8821).
3) Support Ops: add a checklist item for case study metric capture: confirm no maintenance/drain events in the selected interval.

Attachments

- Screenshots of queue depth + p95 charts saved in #support-internal thread (ref: Slack link in comments).

2025-10-09 16:48 UTC — Miguel Santos (Reporter): Opening this because Marketing is collecting Northwind p95 for a public case study this week. Need to confirm whether this is a platform blip and whether to exclude this interval from any published metric.
2025-10-09 16:55 UTC — Simran Kaur (Assignee): Looking at Dedicated overview now. Seeing queue depth climb and ready replicas briefly below desired. No model rollout. Pulling k8s events next.
2025-10-09 17:06 UTC — Simran Kaur: K8s events show a gpu-node drain in nw-dedicated-us-east at ~16:49 UTC. One replica pending longer than usual (image pull). This aligns with p95 spike. Will coordinate with Infra to confirm patch/drain reason and ensure we avoid repeats during measurement.
2025-10-09 17:18 UTC — Markus Klein (Solutions Engineering): Thanks. For the case study we’ll use a rolling 7-day window p95 and add a metrics disclaimer; we will not use the 16:45–17:10 window. Please confirm once mitigations are in place so we can proceed with the interview summary.
2025-10-09 17:42 UTC — Simran Kaur: Mitigation proposal: temporarily raise min_replicas and tighten PDB for Northwind pool; also ask Infra to pause non-urgent maintenance through next Wednesday. Posting details in #support and will update ticket after change.
2025-10-10 14:05 UTC — Simran Kaur: Changes applied: min_replicas 6->8 (business hours), PDB updated. Infra confirmed drain was part of standard kernel patch cycle; they’ve added Northwind pool to a temporary maintenance freeze list through 2025-10-16.
2025-10-12 09:30 UTC — Miguel Santos: Northwind confirmed latency has been stable since Thursday. Closing the loop for Marketing: safe to proceed with publication using rolling window + disclaimer.
Resolved after identifying a transient Dedicated pool capacity reduction due to a GPU node drain/replacement, which temporarily reduced ready replicas and increased queue depth. Applied mitigations (higher min_replicas during business hours, PDB tightening, temporary maintenance freeze) and documented guidance to exclude the affected interval from case study metric capture. No further customer action required.

sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Overload protection operational alerts

Overload protection operational alerts

These are predictive/guardrail alerts. Configure as:

- **Page (Sev2):** enterprise overload shedding sustained
  - enterprise `shed_rate` > **0.1%** for **10 minutes** (any protected route)
- **Ticket:** best-effort shedding unexpectedly high at low utilization

- **Ticket:** queue depth / scheduler lag sustained without corresponding shedding
  - queue depth > threshold for **10 minutes** with `admission_control_active=false` (indicates missing trigger wiring)

sections.section_path: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Summary
sections.heading: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Summary
sections.content:
Summary

On 2026-02-12, the production performance canary generated a burst of false-positive alerts across multiple models and regions shortly after enabling warning + paging rules in the first expansion beyond the initial 2-model rollout. Alerts were high volume (warning + paging) and repeatedly reopened due to dedupe failures, resulting in on-call interruption and a temporary release freeze request.

There was **no confirmed customer-facing latency regression** attributable to this incident. The event was an alerting/observability failure caused primarily by (1) **baseline drift + baseline key mismatch** and (2) **metric label cardinality inflation** that fragmented the canary’s time series, defeating min-sample gating and dedupe.

sections.section_path: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > Severity guidance (SRE)
sections.heading: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > Severity guidance (SRE)
sections.content:
Severity guidance (SRE)

Use the following guidelines when declaring severity:

- **SEV-1:** Widespread routing impact (many tenants), large latency/5xx increase, or rollout control plane causing sustained customer outage.
- **SEV-2:** Single large tenant impacted (SLA risk), or split mismatch causing repeated auto-pauses/rollbacks with user-visible degradation.
- **SEV-3:** Rollout stuck without service impact (customer blocked but production stable) or split mismatch limited to one region with low traffic.

If in doubt and customer-facing impact is ongoing, escalate severity early; mitigation (freeze/rollback) is typically low-risk.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Definitions
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Definitions
sections.content:
Definitions

- **Deployment**: A Dedicated inference endpoint identified by `deployment_id` and bound to a region and hardware pool.
- **Route**: A logical API capability within a deployment (e.g., `chat.completions`, `completions`, `embeddings`). For this SLO, throughput is evaluated at the **deployment level**, with route breakdowns used for diagnostics.
- **Committed Throughput Floor (CTF)**: The minimum throughput Redwood commits to sustain for a deployment under defined conditions. Expressed as **tokens/sec** (canonical) or **requests/sec** (only for non-tokenized routes; see below).
- **Observed Throughput**: Throughput computed from Redwood-side metering and timing, scoped to eligible requests.
- **SLO Window**: The evaluation interval used to determine compliance for a point in time (5 minutes).
- **Error Budget**: The allowed fraction of SLO windows that can be below the committed floor over the compliance period.

- Availability by tier (enterprise vs best-effort)

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
- Today we mostly deny quickly; some customers want queuing.
- SRE view: queuing can hide fleet pain and increase tail; if we add queueing it must be bounded with clear max wait + cancellation and must not break determinism.

2) How much “degraded mode” behavior is acceptable?

- If telemetry is stale, do we:
  a) deny all burst? (safe but may be overly strict)
  b) allow small burst with conservative cap? (better UX)
  c) continue as-is with risk? (not acceptable)
- Tentative: (b) with tight global caps + explicit surfaced state.

3) GA scope: region/hardware allow list

- Recommendation: GA in us-east H100 first; add eu-west after EU-West latency fix + game day rerun.

Appendix: customer support learnings (from tickets)

- SUP-28411 (unexpected denials): customers interpret “burst enabled” as “guaranteed extra capacity.” We must emphasize “best-effort within guardrails,” with clear reasons.
- SUP-28503 (429s): customers need explicit guidance on client-side backoff, concurrency control, and how to detect “you are at cap.”
- SUP-28488 (billing question): customers will audit the burst line item against their own job schedule; we need accurate exports + transparent calculation.

Next steps

- Rafael to turn P0s into a GA gate checklist and review in SRE staff meeting (2025-06-04).
- Schedule a short follow-up retro after GA week 1 to validate assumptions and update runbooks.

sections.section_path: Go Live Protocols Cross Org Communications Escalation 2027
sections.heading: Go Live Protocols Cross Org Communications Escalation 2027
sections.content:
| Level | Trigger example | Primary contact | Secondary contact | Action required |
|-------|-----------------|-----------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| L1 (CSM) | Customer questions, minor errors | CSM | SE | Acknowledge to customer within 15m, open internal thread |
| L2 (SRE) | Error rate >5% | Oncall SRE | SRE Lead | Execute diagnostics, apply mitigations (rate-limit, route switch) |
| L3 (SE/PM) | Persistent degradation >30m | Solutions Engineer | Product Manager | Coordinate config changes, model fallback, communicate to customer executives |
| L4 (Exec) | SLA breach or major incident | Head of Customer Success | Head of Engineering | Declare incident, engage legal/finance if SLA credits likely |

Note: The table above is intended as a quick reference. The full escalation paging list with phone numbers and PagerDuty IDs is stored in /confluence/people-ops/rosters and in the private channel pinned messages.

Common Mitigations (ordered by lowest customer impact first)
----------------------------------------------------------

- Increase routing to a higher-capacity pool (if Dedicated: burst pool)
- Apply tenant-level throttles to protect shared resources (quota reduce to 30% of projected steady-state)
- Enable model fallback: route to last-known-stable model snapshot
- Temporarily switch customer to hosted API endpoint (if allowed by contract)
- Quiesce long-running batch jobs from the customer side

Rollback and Safe-fail Strategies
--------------------------------

1. Safe rollback to previous routing config (SE executes):
   - Command: curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal.redwood/v1/route/revert -d '{"tenant":"<tenant-id>","to_config":"<previous-config-id>"}' 
   - Confirm routing table via: kubectl get svc ingress-<tenant> -o yaml (requires ops role)
2. Tenant quiesce API (customer-facing graceful shutdown):
   - POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/tenants/<tenant>/quiesce?actor=ops
   - Expected behavior: existing requests drain, new requests return 429 with Retry-After header.
3. Emergency switchback to hosted region: update DNS TTL and apply traffic policy TTL=30s for faster re-routing.

Communication Templates
-----------------------

- Customer-facing 1-line (acknowledge): "We are investigating increased latency for your production routes and will provide an update within 15 minutes. No action required from your side unless we ask."
- Customer-facing status update (10m cadence): include short bullet list: observed metric, action taken, owner, ETA for next update.
- Internal P0 page message sample:
  - "P0: <customer> production routes returning 503s since 08:12 UTC. Oncall SRE investigating. Initial hypothesis: ingress proxy thread exhaustion. Paging SRE Lead and SE. Next update in 5 minutes"

Telemetry checks / Queries (examples)
----------------------------------

- PromQL (errors): sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[5m])) > 0.05
- Token consumption anomaly (example):
  - Query: increase(token_count_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[30m]) / expected_token_rate > 2.0
- Synthetic validation command (curl):
  - curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -d '{"input":"synthetic health check"}' | jq '.latency_ms'

Post-Cutover (T+4 to T+72 hours)
--------------------------------

- Stability window monitoring: SRE to keep watch for 72 hours; escalate on any SLO breach.
- Cost and quota reconciliation: Finance Ops and CSM to review token consumption, forecast delta, and apply quota protections if needed.
- Customer QBR prep: collect first-week metrics and any incident notes for the 30-day QBR.

Runbook Ownership and RACI
-------------------------

sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > General notes
sections.content:
SLOs (targets)

General notes

- SLOs are evaluated over a **rolling 28-day window**.
- Unless specified, targets apply per region (e.g., us-east, eu-west).
- We define both **p95 and p99** latency objectives for enterprise; best-effort uses p95 as primary.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Saturation requirement (practical interpretation)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Saturation requirement (practical interpretation)
sections.content:
Saturation requirement (practical interpretation)

This SLO is designed to answer: “When the customer is **trying** to use their Dedicated capacity, do we deliver the committed throughput?”

Therefore, compliance reporting only considers periods where the deployment is **meaningfully loaded**.

We define “meaningfully loaded” for a window as:

- `eligible_generation_wall_time_seconds >= 120` seconds within the 5-minute window

If a window does not meet the load threshold, it is treated as **insufficient demand** and excluded from compliance (removed from total). This prevents underutilized deployments from producing misleading ‘low throughput’ windows.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Computation > Fixed baseline artifact
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Computation > Fixed baseline artifact
sections.content:
Baseline Computation

Fixed baseline artifact

- Source: controlled perf-canary runs using the approved synthetic prompt distribution.
- For each baseline key, we store:
  - distribution summaries (p50/p95/p99) for each latency metric
  - mean and standard deviation where stable enough to be meaningful
  - tokens/sec distribution summaries
  - run metadata (time range, sample count, canary config version)
- Baseline validity: baseline is considered valid only if it meets minimum sample size requirements (see below) and passes sanity checks (no telemetry gaps, no error-rate spikes).

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.content:
What changed (customer-facing)

When the platform is saturated (GPU capacity, scheduler backlog, downstream dependency brownout), Redwood may reject requests *early* and predictably rather than allowing them to time out or generate random 5xx.

Customers may now see:

- **429** responses for admission / quota / per-tenant caps.
- **503** responses when a regional/model circuit breaker is open or the system is actively shedding load.

These responses:

- Include stable **error codes** and a machine-readable JSON payload.
- Typically include a **Retry-After** header to indicate safe retry timing.
- Include Redwood request/correlation IDs for tracing.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Positive
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Positive
sections.content:
Consequences

Positive

- Earlier, clearer shedding reduces tail latency and incident severity.
- Tenant/tier fairness is enforced consistently at the edge.
- Runtime remains protected even if gateway/routing misestimate load.
- Routing provides graceful degradation (fallback) without turning into a retry storm engine.

sections.section_path: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Context / problem
sections.heading: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Context / problem
sections.content:
Context / problem

Hosted canary rollouts require percentage-based traffic splitting on a Hosted route (e.g., 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%) while maintaining:

- Consistent cohorting so a given end user/conversation does not “flip” unpredictably
- Correctness under retries, streaming, and regional failover
- Clear metrics for baseline vs canary cohorts (including when the system must fall back)

Constraints:

- Data plane enforcement must be fast and operate without a central “assignment service.”
- Region routing and model fallback already exist; cohorting must compose cleanly.
- Customers may or may not provide stable end-user identifiers.

sections.section_path: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Initial support response (guidance provided)
sections.heading: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Initial support response (guidance provided)
sections.content:
Initial support response (guidance provided)

- Confirmed that the new system returns distinct reason codes and customers should key their retry/backoff behavior on:
  - "quota_exceeded" (respect quota windows; reduce steady-state rate)
  - "overload_protection_admission" (transient overload; respect Retry-After; use exponential backoff + jitter)
- Recommended changes:
  - Use exponential backoff with full jitter; cap concurrency; do not retry immediately.
  - Honor Retry-After; treat 429 as a signal to shed load client-side.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 1) Availability SLI (server success)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 1) Availability SLI (server success)
sections.content:
1) Availability SLI (server success)

**Definition:** percentage of requests that return an eligible success response.

- Success codes: `2xx` (and `3xx` if any internal redirects apply; typically none)
- Failures: `5xx`, `408`, `499` (client disconnect) are counted as failures unless explicitly excluded by route-specific rules below.

**Tier handling of 429:**

- **Enterprise:** `429` due to *overload shedding/admission control* counts as **unavailable** (because enterprise is protected; overload shed should be rare and indicates under-provisioning or misconfiguration).
- **Best-effort:** `429` due to overload shedding/admission control does **not** count as unavailable (it is expected behavior under pressure). Quota/rate-limit 429s are not counted as availability failures for either tier.

**Note:** 429 classification must be based on the reason code emitted by gateway/policy engine, not inferred from rate.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.content:
Alternatives considered

1) **Single global breaker at gateway only**

- Rejected: insufficient fidelity; cannot protect runtime safety in all cases; still allows deep queueing.

2) **Runtime-only backpressure (let everything in)**

- Rejected: overload manifests as queued latency/timeouts; poor customer semantics; wastes upstream work.

3) **Routing-driven global admission control**

- Rejected: routing is not the best place to enforce tenant fairness and local dependency breakers; risks complex control loops.

Satellite Grove

Lead source: self-serve signup (product-led). Team: CTO (Aisha Kaur), Eng Lead (Mateo Lopez), PM (Rina Shah). Early discovery call 2026-03-02 via Fireflies ff-20260302-0934. Summary: building an in-app conversational assistant for their B2B workflow SaaS; must feel instant (streaming responses) and run on public cloud.

Key requirements:

- Streaming websocket support + chunked tokens (UX requires UI tokens arrive in <50ms increments).
- p50 target ~40-80ms, p95 <120ms, p99 <200ms for short responses (avg 60 tokens).
- Concurrent active users at launch ~100-200, expected steady-state 20-50.
- Cost-sensitive: want guidance on batching vs streaming tradeoffs and token/unit price impact.

POC/workflow discussed:

- Interested in Redwood Optimize suggestions (batching hints, prefix caching) to reduce cost without hurting streaming UX.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > Latency SLOs by route and tier
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > Latency SLOs by route and tier
sections.content:
Latency SLOs by route and tier

Latency objectives are defined in terms of:

- **Chat streaming:** TTFB p95/p99
- **Non-streaming:** E2E p95/p99

| Route | Tier | Latency SLO (primary) | Latency SLO (secondary) | Measurement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | TTFB p95 ≤ 450ms | TTFB p99 ≤ 900ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Best-effort | TTFB p95 ≤ 900ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1800ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (non-streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 1.8s | E2E p99 ≤ 3.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 350ms | E2E p99 ≤ 800ms | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 700ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 550ms | E2E p99 ≤ 1.2s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 1.2s | (informational) p99 ≤ 2.5s | Gateway E2E |

**Notes / caveats**

- Latency SLOs assume nominal prompt and response sizes. Excessive prompt length or extreme max_tokens increases may be subject to policy limits; those requests are still included in latency metrics unless explicitly rejected by policy.
- Where fallback is permitted (route/model policy), latency SLI measures the actual served path; dashboards must annotate fallback activations.

1) Use the customer's traffic shape: 100 concurrent short chat requests (avg 50ms) + 20 parallel multipart embedding uploads (avg 45s each).
2) Route both traffic shapes through the dedicated pool dp-132-usw with current priority-class config (default: interactive=high, background=low).
3) Start background uploads in a tight window to simulate a scheduled flush (cron at 09:00).
4) Observe 429s on interactive calls between 09:00-09:30 when background uploads ramp up.

High - user-visible errors for real-time chat during scheduled bulk ingest; customer is on dedicated tier and requests urgent guidance (P1).
Instructed customer to stagger background multipart uploads and introduce jitter in their flush window. Recommended reducing concurrency of background upload workers to < 6 during peak windows as a temporary mitigation.
2026-03-10 09:20 - Support (Ava Chen): Acknowledged ticket and requested full request IDs and example request traces. Asked customer to confirm whether they use signed URLs for chunk upload callbacks.
2026-03-10 10:05 - Customer (Streamly AI - ops@streamly.ai): Provided request IDs and stated they use signed URLs for chunk completion callbacks and run a cron flush at 09:00 local. Attached sample batch IDs: batch-20260310-0919.
2026-03-10 11:00 - SRE (Liam O'Neill): Checked rate-limiter logs and saw route-level token depletion aligning with the cron flush. Noted some refill events lagged due to burst-pool-weight recalculation on pool attach.
2026-03-11 08:45 - Eng (Maya Patel): Observed a potential priority-class weight inversion in canary release 1.14.0-canary where background ingestion borrow logic could erroneously draw from interactive burst credits under certain attach sequences.
2026-03-12 09:00 - Support (Ava Chen): Shared recommended config changes and rollout plan. Scheduling a brief call with customer for 2026-03-12 14:00 PDT to apply non-breaking adjustments and observe behavior.
2026-03-12 13:30 - Customer (Streamly AI): Agreed to the windowed-stagger plan and will apply client-side jitter for the March 12 trial.
1) Correlation between cron flush start times and onset of 429s is strong (observability traces + rate-limiter counters).
2) Rate-limiter metric rlim.route.tokens.available shows transient negative deltas when background workers register multiple concurrent signed-url callbacks (double-counting observed in edge proxy earlier; needs validation).
3) Canary release 1.14.0 has a code path that recalculates burst-pool weights when a route attaches to a new pool; race condition can allow an attach to read stale bucket state and permit borrow that appears to zero out another pool's credits.
4) Some 429s are opaque because edge proxy returns before rate-limiter headers are populated when under heavy callback fanout. Need to instrument edge path to surface X-RateLimit headers even under backpressure.
5) No evidence of dedicated pool GPU exhaustion; autoscaler metrics are stable.
1) Short-term (apply during call): adjust per-route burst allocation to reserve 20% of interactive burst credits exclusively for priority=high routes on dp-132-usw.
2) Short-term: recommend customer stagger flush windows and add randomized jitter to callback fanout.

sections.heading: Sup 18510 Streaming Throughput Metric Mismatch
sections.content:
Sup 18510 Streaming Throughput Metric Mismatch

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_a5a5235d973e421c870e11ceea4887ed
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Streaming throughput metric mismatch (customer dashboard vs Redwood export) — suspected token accounting double-count in streaming

Customer (Vidorama) reports inconsistent throughput numbers for their Dedicated deployment when using streaming responses.

Issue summary

- Vidorama is comparing:
  1) Redwood Console throughput panel (tokens/sec) for their Dedicated deployment, and
  2) Their internal measurement based on streamed tokens (client-side) + Redwood usage export.
- They see Redwood Console tokens/sec ~1.8–2.1x higher than their client-side computed throughput for the same time windows.
- Discrepancy appears only for streaming (non-streaming requests match within ~5–10%).

Impact

- Customer confusion + concern about Dedicated throughput SLO reporting accuracy.
- Potential false positives/negatives in SLO compliance if the canonical throughput metric is inflated for streaming.

Customer-provided details

- Workload: chat completions, streaming enabled (server-sent events).
- Typical request: prompt 1–2k tokens, completion 150–400 tokens, 20–60 concurrent streams.
- Sampling window: 5-min rolling, comparing against their Prometheus counters.

Redwood initial checks (Support)

- Confirmed customer is hitting the correct deployment_id and region (us-east).
- Confirmed they are not mixing model variants in the comparison window (pinned to llama-3.1-70b-instruct; occasional mixtral bursts were excluded by customer).
- Confirmed they are not counting input tokens in their client throughput metric (they only count generated tokens).

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1) Run load test against a Dedicated deployment with streaming enabled.
2) Compare:

   - streaming token counter used by throughput dashboard (server-side), vs
   - sum(completion_tokens) from request final usage events (server-side) and/or reconstructed deltas.

3) Observe that for streaming requests, the dashboard-aligned metric increases faster than final usage totals.

Investigation notes (SRE/Obs)

- Hypothesis A: double-counting streamed completion tokens (both per-chunk deltas and final usage event contribute to the same counter).
- Hypothesis B: retries/resumes on stream reconnects cause duplicated deltas.
- Hypothesis C: mixed attribution labels (route vs deployment) cause aggregation overlap.

Findings

- We can reproduce consistent ~2x inflation when streaming is enabled and client consumes the full stream.
- Root cause identified in telemetry emission path:
  - For streaming responses, we emit per-chunk token deltas (used for near-real-time throughput).
  - At stream termination, a final usage event is emitted.
  - In the current pipeline, the dashboard throughput counter was incremented by BOTH the per-chunk deltas and the final usage event for the same request.
- This does NOT affect billing totals (billing uses finalized usage only). It affects the real-time throughput metric used in dashboards and SLO evaluation.

Workaround (until fix rollout)

- For customer reporting, use finalized completion token metrics (request end) for streaming workloads:
  - completion_tokens_total (finalized) / wall time
- Avoid using real-time streaming throughput panel for contractual/SLO comparisons until patched.

Next actions

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.content:
Streaming-specific guidance

Streaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.

- Recommend **lower streaming concurrency** during peak periods.
- If the customer can tolerate it, recommend **shorter outputs** (reduce `max_tokens`) and/or **shorter prompts**.
- If a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.

sections.content:
Sliced Ingest 429S Dedicated Pool Priority Class Debug Notes

Source type: google_drive
Document ID: dsid_8ffbd9fe82df457ca67d4fbc9ff1090c
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Sliced ingest 429s on dedicated pool after migration — priority class + burst pool debug notes (Streamly AI)

Context / why this doc exists

- This is a working scratchpad for SRE/Eng while debugging Streamly AI’s sustained 429s during sliced ingest after dedicated pool migration.
- Source ticket: SUP-864999 (customer-support). This doc is meant to be the “newer truth” vs the older ticket narrative since we’ve learned more post-call + after patch testing.

Customer + impact recap (same as ticket, but condensed)

- Customer: Streamly AI (dedicated tier)
- Environment: prod us-west, dedicated pool dp-132-usw
- Traffic mix:
  - Interactive: short chat calls (priority=high)
  - Background: multipart embedding uploads (priority=background/low) with signed URL chunk completion callbacks
- Observed on 2026-03-10 ~09:00–11:30 PDT:
  - ~30% of short chat requests returned 429 coincident with the scheduled bulk ingest flush
  - Customer saw retry amplification and user-visible errors

Versions / components

- Dedicated pool: dp-132-usw
- Ingest coordinator version (at time of incident): 2026.02.3
- Rate-limiter version (at time of incident): 1.14.0-canary
- Edge / API gateway involved due to opaque 429 behavior (missing headers)

Symptoms (what we saw)

- Persistent 429s for /v1/chat during background upload ramp.
- Throttle headers when present indicated per-route window exhaustion.
- A subset of 429s were “opaque” (no X-RateLimit headers) especially during callback fanout peaks.

Example log snippets (from ticket; kept here for reference)

- 2026-03-10T09:02:14Z - 200 - /v1/chat - key=acct-streamly-01 - latency=62ms
- 2026-03-10T09:02:19Z - 429 - /v1/chat - key=acct-streamly-01 - throttle: route_window=0/100
- 2026-03-10T09:02:20Z - 429 - /v1/embed - key=acct-streamly-01 - chunk=12/20 - err=quota_exhausted
- 2026-03-10T09:05:01Z - 429 - /v1/chat - key=acct-streamly-01 - no-rate-headers (opaque)

Steps to reproduce (traffic shape)
1) 100 concurrent short chat requests (avg 50ms) + 20 parallel multipart embedding uploads (avg 45s each).
2) Route both traffic shapes through dp-132-usw with priority classes: interactive=high, background=low.
3) Start background uploads in tight window (cron-style flush ~09:00 local).
4) Observe interactive 429s during the first 20–40 minutes of background ramp.

What changed vs initial hypothesis (updated findings)

- Initial hypothesis in SUP-864999: “priority class mismatch / weight inversion in 1.14.0-canary allows background to borrow interactive burst credits under certain attach sequences.”
- Updated after deeper review (2026-03-13 to 2026-03-20):
  - There are TWO overlapping issues:
    (A) Rate-limiter burst-pool attach race (real) that can temporarily mis-attribute available burst credits across pools.
    (B) Edge proxy early-return path under backpressure causing missing X-RateLimit headers and (worse) collapsing distinct upstream 429 reasons into a single opaque 429 surface.
  - The attach race (A) increases the probability that interactive tokens are temporarily depleted during the exact window when callback fanout is max.
  - The edge behavior (B) makes it look like “random 429s” and prevents the customer from applying correct retry/backoff logic.

Root cause (current best explanation)

sections.content:
Sup 3812 Northwind Dedicated Latency Spike During Interview Window

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_0c504258cd0c432d898e6711fb90eaf6
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Northwind Commerce (Dedicated): transient p95 latency spike during case study measurement/interview window

Issue summary

- Northwind Commerce noticed an elevated p95 latency window on their Dedicated cluster while Marketing/SE were collecting performance numbers for a planned public case study.
- The spike was transient (~18 minutes) but would materially change any "single-window" p95 figure if captured during that interval.

Customer impact

- Endpoint: /v1/chat.completions (streaming + non-streaming)
- Impact: p95 increased from baseline ~430–520ms to ~1.6–2.1s; p99 peaked ~3.8s.
- Error rate: no sustained 5xx increase; brief uptick in 429s due to queue protection (max in-flight).
- User-visible symptoms: slower first-token latency on some requests; a few retries observed by Northwind.

Context (why ticket was opened)

- This was surfaced during case study preparation (interview + metric capture). We need to:
  1) confirm whether the spike was a platform issue vs workload change,
  2) ensure mitigations prevent recurrence during future measurement windows,
  3) document the event so published metrics are measured over an appropriate window (e.g., 7–30 days) and/or exclude known maintenance events.

Timeline (UTC)

- 2025-10-09 16:42: Northwind reports "latency feels off" in Slack via CSM; SE flags risk to published p95.
- 16:46: Support opens SUP-3812; on-call begins triage.
- 16:50–17:08: p95 elevated; queue depth rises; autoscaler events noted.
- 17:10: Tail latency returns to baseline without customer changes.
- 17:35: Initial hypothesis shared with SE/Marketing; agree to avoid quoting that window.

Observability / dashboards

- Dedicated overview (Grafana): https://grafana.redwoodinference.com/d/ded-nw/northwind-dedicated-overview?from=2025-10-09T16:30:00Z&to=2025-10-09T18:00:00Z
- API p95 by route (Datadog): https://app.datadoghq.com/dashboard/3xq-9qk-7eu/northwind-api-latency?from_ts=1760027400000&to_ts=1760032800000
- Scheduler queue depth: https://grafana.redwoodinference.com/d/sched-q/scheduler-queue-depth?var=cluster=northwind-dedicated-us-east
- Node events (maintenance/drain): https://grafana.redwoodinference.com/d/k8s-ev/k8s-events?var=namespace=nw-dedicated

What we checked

- Workload: No evidence of a step-function traffic increase from Northwind; request rate remained within typical burst bounds (+8% vs same weekday baseline).
- Model/version: No model rollout; pinned model version unchanged.
- Platform: K8s events showed a single GPU node drain/replace in the Dedicated pool coincident with the spike.

Investigation notes (most likely cause)

- Root cause: transient capacity reduction during a node drain (kernel security patch) combined with conservative surge settings for the deployment, leading to fewer ready replicas for ~10–15 minutes.
- Contributing factors:
  - Warm-up for the replacement node took longer than expected (image pull + cache warm), increasing request queue depth.
  - Autoscaler reacted, but scale-up lag (GPU provisioning) meant tail latency increased before capacity stabilized.

Mitigation applied

- Short-term (same day):
  - Increased min_replicas for Northwind Dedicated deployment from 6 -> 8 during business hours.
  - Adjusted pod disruption budget to reduce simultaneous unready capacity during drains.
  - Coordinated with Infra to pause non-urgent maintenance on Northwind’s Dedicated pool during the case study measurement week.
- Follow-up hardening:
  - Added an alert on "ready replicas < desired" + queue depth correlation for Dedicated clusters.
  - Documented recommended measurement window guidance for Marketing/SE: use rolling 7-day p95 (excluding maintenance/drain events) or present a range with a footnote.

Customer comms

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 7) Mitigation options you can offer immediately (tier-dependent)
sections.content:
7) Mitigation options you can offer immediately (tier-dependent)

These are customer-facing actions CS/Support may propose, with SRE confirmation where possible:

- Temporarily reduce max context / max output tokens (if within acceptable product behavior).
- Temporarily shift traffic to the contracted primary route only (avoid experimental routes).
- Enable/disable streaming based on their client constraints (note: streaming affects perceived latency but should not invalidate throughput).
- If the customer has multi-deployment setup: fail over to a secondary deployment (Premium: may be Redwood-assisted).

Do not promise failover across regions unless the tier/contract explicitly includes it.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > C. Streaming responses — how to describe
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > C. Streaming responses — how to describe
sections.content:
C. Streaming responses — how to describe

**Approved clause (standard):**
“For streaming responses, usage is measured based on tokens processed and reported by Redwood for the request. If a streaming connection is interrupted, Redwood may report usage for tokens processed up to the point of interruption.”

**Negotiation notes:**

- Avoid promising that interrupted streams are always free; we can grant credits case-by-case.

sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Metrics Covered
sections.content:
Metrics Covered

Baselines and regressions are computed for:

- End-to-end latency: p50, p95, p99 (ms)
- Runtime-only latency: p50, p95, p99 (ms) (excludes network/client)
- Prefill latency and decode latency (ms)
- Queueing time (ms) (scheduler-level)
- Tokens/sec (overall, and decode tokens/sec where available)
- Batch size distribution (for attribution)
- KV cache hit rate (where applicable; informational at v1)

Incident Bot: :rotating_light: *INCIDENT* (beta) - "rollout split mismatch" reported by Northstar in us-east. Expected canary=10%, observed ~35-45% over last 10m. Route: `hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod`. Rollout: `rlt_7f2c`.

`sum(rate(rw_infer_requests_total{route="hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod",region="us-east",cohort="canary"}[5m])) / sum(rate(rw_infer_requests_total{route="hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod",region="us-east"}[5m]))`

Rafael Mendes: ack. is this impacting latency/error? customer-facing impact?

Sean Gallagher: error rate stable, but this is a safety issue if the new model is bad. We should treat as sev2-ish for beta. Let's contain.

Mina Haddad: on it. This is traffic-splitting enforcement in data plane. If it’s only us-east, could be hash input mismatch on that cluster or a config propagation issue.

Ravi Menon: +1. First check: are we using the same `cohort_key` in us-east? It’s supposed to be `tenant_id + route_id + stable_user_key` with fallback to request_id if missing.

Emily Zhao: I can check the us-east router build / config digest. Might be running slightly different commit?

Rafael Mendes: mitigation: can we pause rollout / force canary=0 in us-east only?

Hannah Rivera: orchestrator supports pause globally; region-scoped override is behind flag but I think Smart Routing has region weights per rollout? Mina confirm.

Mina Haddad: yes, routing primitive has per-region enforcement weights. Quickest is set canary weight to 0 in us-east (keep 10% elsewhere). Alternatively pause the rollout which sets all regions to baseline.

Elena Popov: I can push a config patch to set `regions.us-east.canary_pct=0` for rlt_7f2c. Will take ~2-3 mins to propagate.

Dylan Brooks: FYI Console shows rollout at step 10% with soak timer running. If we do region override, Console won’t reflect it yet (known gap). Marissa: heads up.

Marissa Cole: yep, understood. For beta customer safety > UI accuracy. We’ll message Northstar through support channel.

Rafael Mendes: +1. Let’s do it.
Elena Popov: applying patch now.

Incident Bot: Change requested by @Elena Popov: "Set rlt_7f2c canary_pct=0 in us-east" (config pipeline: `routing-prod`).

rollout_id=rlt_7f2c route=hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod region=us-east
cohort_key_source=header:x-rw-user-key
cohort_key_present=false
fallback_source=ip

That looks suspicious: `hash_seed=route_id_only`??? should include tenant_id at least.

Ravi Menon: whoa. That `hash_seed` field indicates the "v0" cohorting code path. That would skew based on NAT IP distribution too.

Emily Zhao: checking build stamp in us-east: it’s on `router@1.38.2` but others are `1.38.3`. us-east missed the rollout during last deploy window.

Mina Haddad: ok so we have version skew. 1.38.2 uses legacy cohorting fallback behavior (route-only seed when user key missing). That can absolutely produce mismatch.

- Profile: Horizon Quay is a global maritime logistics SaaS (port ops + scheduling). Heavy real-time chat+assistant for ops centers; embeddings for manifest search; reranking for ETA predictions.
- Capacity ask: Reserved pool sized for 8 sustained A100-equivalent GPUs per primary region (NA + EU). Expected steady-state: ~350–600 RPS for short payload chat (avg token window 256). Burst to ~1k RPS during shift changes.
- Performance targets: P95 text-gen latency <= 80ms, P99 <= 220ms for chat on dedicated pool; throughput guarantees of 500 RPS sustained per region.
- SLA position (customer asks): 99.95% uptime across dedicated pools; 30% credit at 99.9–99.95; 50% credit below 99.9; request for monthly credit cap and cumulative measurement window.
- Redwood counterproposals discussed: baseline 99.95 SLA with quarterly reconciliation; credit schedule tiered: 99.9–99.95 = 10% service credit, 99.5–99.9 = 30%, <99.5 = 60% (proposal to legal). Redwood wants max cap at 6 months' fee.

- Support / escalation: Horizon Quay requires 24/7 hotline for Sev1 with 15-minute acknowledgement, 2-hour remediate SLA target for critical infrastructure, 4-hour for Sev2. Redwood proposes 15min ack, 1h initial response, remediation time objective to be defined per incident severity in SOW.
- Throughput guarantees & reserved GPU planning: plan includes capacity buffer for 1.5x expected steady-state; autoscaling burst into shared pool allowed with pre-authorized fallback; need explicit routing policy for latency-first vs cost-first (customer wants latency-first for ops-critical calls).

- POC summary (3 weeks):
  * Week 0: onboarding, network peering, SSO test (SAML).

  * Week 2: load testing to 1.2x forecast, KV/prefix cache tuning, batch tuning.

- POC status: onboarding complete; peering and SSO in staging done; load tests scheduled 2026-03-15. Initial latency targets met on small-scale tests; sustained throughput test pending.
- Procurement notes: finance wants committed capacity discount tiers and an option to convert to Dedicated Reserved on annual renewal. Legal flagged service credit language and liability cap.
- Quote history: pricing deck sent 2026-02-28 (drive link). Redwood gave two sizing options: 8x reserved (latency-priority) and 12x with burst (cost amortized). Horizon Quay prefers 8x + autoscale to shared.
- Direct quotes from stakeholders: "We cannot accept blackouts during port shift windows — any maintenance must be out of peak or have a clear failover plan." — Head of Ops.

sections.heading: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > Symptoms and likely causes > B) Traffic split mismatch
sections.content:
B) Traffic split mismatch

**Common symptoms:**

- Observed canary traffic differs significantly from configured percent.
- Split matches overall, but **per-region** mismatch (e.g., us-east OK, eu-west off).
- Mismatch only for streaming requests or retries.
- Canary sees 0% traffic despite non-zero configuration.

**Likely causes:**

- Deterministic cohort key mismatch (unexpected hashing input due to missing user/session key).
- Sticky assignment changes across retries (incorrect retry key usage).
- Multi-region propagation lag (config not yet applied everywhere).
- Data plane caching old route config.
- A/B test or fallback routing policy taking precedence (policy evaluation order).

---

Int 9821 Crucible Inference Latency Spike And 5Xx Inc 9821

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_0c1f1c83e8d44d2fa3a9f6c7b2d7b9f1
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Crucible Health: inference latency spike + transient 5xx on /v1/generate (INC-9821)

Customer escalation relayed by Stephanie Nguyen. Crucible Health reported sudden latency spike and burst of 5xx on inference endpoint /v1/generate beginning ~2026-08-28 07:55 PDT. Reported impact: median latency increased from ~120ms to ~900ms; throughput dropped from ~250 req/s to ~150 req/s for Crucible production key; initial customer-observed 5xx rate ~8% during the window; multiple batches timed out and downstream throttles triggered. Customer had a critical demo at 10:00 PDT.

Immediate hypotheses (serving): autoscaler oscillation under burst + degraded single shard causing head-of-line blocking.

Immediate mitigations executed: emergency scale-up of dedicated pool (target +20% capacity) + temporary concurrency limit increase + drain suspected bad instance(s) + enable routing of new requests to compatible fallback model variant (lower context) to reduce per-token work.

Outcome (updated after investigation): improvements observed within ~9–12 minutes; throughput returned to baseline and tail latency normalized after draining the degraded node(s) and reverting autoscaler policy.

Updated root cause (post-incident): the triggering event was an autoscaler policy update that reduced stabilization/cooldown and interacted poorly with a burst in queue depth, causing scale oscillation. One GPU instance concurrently entered a degraded driver state (intermittent kernel launch stalls rather than a hard OOM), amplifying tail latency and increasing request timeouts which surfaced as 5xx at the gateway. The instance replacement lag plus oscillation extended the incident duration.

sections.content:
Page 4: Evaluation best practices

**Proposed title:** “How to evaluate quality and latency before rollout”

**Customer-friendly guidance**

- Suggested evaluation approach:
  - Identify representative prompts (production samples + edge cases).
  - Run baseline vs profile-enabled comparisons.
  - Use A/B sampling (e.g., 1–5% traffic) with a rollback threshold.

- What to measure
  - Quality: task-specific metrics (pass@k, exact match, ranking metrics) + human review where appropriate.
  - Latency: p50/p95 decode latency and time-to-first-token.
  - Cost: cost/token and throughput.

- Rollout strategy
  1) Enable in staging on a non-critical route
  2) Canary in production (small % traffic)
  3) Expand gradually with monitoring

- Provide explicit “stop conditions”
  - Elevated fallback rate
  - Increased error rate
  - Statistically meaningful quality regression on a defined slice

**Note:** We cannot publish Redwood’s internal thresholds verbatim if they are considered sensitive, but we can publish recommended guardrails (e.g., “predefine acceptable deltas and require sign-off”). We will align with Selene Huang (quality guardrails) on what’s safe to disclose.
