sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Redlines: common asks and recommended responses > 2) “Do not charge for retries / failed requests.”
sections.content:
2) “Do not charge for retries / failed requests.”

**Position:** If compute is performed, some usage may be reported.
**Response:** Use idempotency + commercially reasonable efforts clause. Offer a credits mechanism for verified platform-caused duplicate charges.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Rollout Guidance
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Rollout Guidance
sections.content:
Rollout Guidance

- Phase 1 (single region): warnings only, tune per-model overrides until noise is acceptable.
- Phase 2: enable paging only for top models with proven low variance and stable baselines.
- Phase 3: integrate gating with release engineering once paging signal is trusted (warning can gate early as “soft fail,” paging as “hard fail”).

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > C) Per-region baselines always on
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > C) Per-region baselines always on
sections.content:
C) Per-region baselines always on

Pros:

- Reduces false positives due to cross-region fleet differences.

Cons:

- Baseline explosion (more artifacts and config), operational overhead.

Decision: Region is optional and only enabled for models/regions where observed variance requires it.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)
sections.content:
Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)

These are emitted to dashboards and included in alert payloads, but do not page unless explicitly enabled for a model:

- Queueing time p95 +25% (suggests scheduler/fleet saturation)
- Prefill p95 +15% (suggests kernel/model config regressions)
- Decode p95 +15% (suggests kernel/model config regressions)

Rationale:

- Paging should be driven by end-to-end customer-impact proxy (E2E p95 and tokens/sec).
- Breakdown metrics improve triage but are often noisier and more sensitive to load mix.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > G. Measurement system and authoritative records
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > G. Measurement system and authoritative records
sections.content:
G. Measurement system and authoritative records

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Fees are based on Redwood’s measurement systems and usage records. Redwood will provide usage reporting via invoice detail, Console, or usage export/API. In the event of conflict, the invoice and supporting usage report for the billing period will control, subject to Customer’s dispute rights.”

sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Redlines: common asks and recommended responses > 3) “Caching must always reduce price.”
sections.content:
3) “Caching must always reduce price.”

**Position:** Caching may reduce billed tokens depending on eligibility and product policy.
**Response:** Use caching clause; avoid hard commitments. If needed for the deal, define a limited-term promotional adjustment with Finance sign-off.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 2) “Request”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 2) “Request”
sections.content:
2) “Request”

A **Request** is an API call that is accepted by Redwood’s service and results in an attempt to process the call (including streaming requests). Do not tie “request” to “successful response” unless Product/Finance explicitly approves.

sections.section_path: 20260828 Crucible Inference Sitrep
sections.heading: 20260828 Crucible Inference Sitrep
sections.content:
Root cause: A recently deployed autoscaler policy update combined with a rare kernel failure on a single GPU instance produced cascading queue pressure; autoscaler oscillation and a lag in instance replacement led to transient 5xxs and reduced throughput. The failing instance also intermittently returned degraded kernel performance which amplified tail latency.

What we did:

- Emergency capacity bump and routing to fallback model variant on 2026-08-28 at 08:28 PDT — immediate tail-latency improved and throughput returned to baseline within ~12 minutes.
- Drained and reprovisioned the failing instance; patched the kernel path in the affected image and rolled a hotfix to prevent identical failures.
- Reverted the autoscaler policy update and introduced a short cool-down to prevent oscillation.

Impact:

- Customer observed peak 5xx rate of 8% and throughput drop to ~60% of baseline for a ~10-minute window. No customer data exfiltration.

Next steps / action items: 
1) We will publish a short postmortem to the customer by EOD with the timeline and mitigations (Hannah + Stephanie).
2) Engineering (Marcus) to harden autoscaler policy testing and add a canary step for autoscaler changes.
3) Product to add a routing knob for immediate cross-model fallback triggered by SLA breach (Marcus + Product).
4) Finance to confirm priority-burst billing terms for this incident (Laura).

Attachments: postmortem-draft.md, kpi_before_after.png

Thanks everyone for the quick triage. Julia — we are sending a tailored postmortem and are happy to run a joint technical review next week if you'd like.

— Marcus Lin
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime
marcus_lin@redwood.com

> > Hi Julia / Ravi — quick update from Redwood...

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)
sections.content:
B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)

Pros:

- Extremely stable; easy to reason about.

Cons:

- Becomes stale as fleet/hardware/driver changes accumulate; increases false positives over time.
- Forces frequent manual work to remain relevant.

Decision: Rejected as the only strategy. Adopted as primary baseline with explicit regeneration workflows.

sections.section_path: 1740726110 Rollout Split Mismatch Us East
sections.heading: 1740726110 Rollout Split Mismatch Us East
sections.content:
Sean Gallagher: root cause candidate: us-east routers running old version, using IP fallback and route-only seed => canary assignment biased.

Aisha Bello: config patch has landed. Observed canary pct in us-east is dropping: 0.22 -> 0.11 over last 2m.

Elena Popov: confirming propagation complete on all us-east POPs. should converge to ~0 within a few mins.

Rafael Mendes: good containment. Next action: get us-east routers to 1.38.3 ASAP.

Emily Zhao: I can kick a redeploy for us-east only. Need release channel sign-off since we’re mid-beta.

Sean Gallagher: do it. This is safety-related.

Incident Bot: :information_source: Deployment requested: `router` to `us-east` version `1.38.3` (requested by @Emily Zhao).

Hannah Rivera: meanwhile I’ll pause the orchestrator step timer? If Console is still counting soak at 10% but us-east is effectively 0, it may confuse auto-stop logic.

Aisha Bello: auto-stop checks are per-region AND global? Right now stop-condition evaluator is using global aggregates with region tag optional. For this rollout we set `regions=["us-east","us-west","eu-central"]` but evaluator is looking at all regions combined.

Sean Gallagher: so with us-east at 0 canary, global canary traffic decreases, which could extend time to significance. That’s ok short-term.

Mina Haddad: agreed; don’t pause orchestrator unless necessary. Just note in activity log / internal timeline.

Marissa Cole: I’ll DM support to tell Northstar “we temporarily disabled canary in us-east while we fix routing layer, no action needed.”

sections.section_path: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > What happened (symptoms)
sections.heading: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > What happened (symptoms)
sections.content:
What happened (symptoms)

The canary’s regression evaluator compared observed p95 latency/tokens-sec against per-model baselines. After model expansion:

- Many evaluations used **fallback baseline values** because the baseline lookup key did not match (baseline existed under a different dimension set).
- Metric series were fragmented by high-cardinality labels; the regression evaluator saw many “small-N” series and oscillated between “enough samples” and “not enough samples” depending on which series was queried.
- Alert rules did not consistently enforce **minimum sample size across the same grouping** used by the evaluator, which allowed small, noisy slices to trip thresholds.
- incident-bot dedupe keys lacked stable identifiers for (model, version, region, sku, runtime_build), so the same underlying symptom created repeated threads/pages.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Context
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Context
sections.content:
Context

Redwood Inference’s Hosted API sees bursty and highly variable traffic (prompt length variance, streaming concurrency spikes, regional capacity dips). During overload, failures can cascade into:

- Tail-latency blowups (p95/p99), then timeouts
- Elevated 5xx from upstream retry storms and downstream saturation
- Noisy-neighbor effects across tenants and tiers
- Confusing customer experience (timeouts and generic 5xx instead of stable semantics)

We need a layered admission control strategy that:
1) Rejects or degrades traffic early and predictably.
2) Preserves tenant isolation and tier-aware behavior.
3) Avoids feedback loops (e.g., shedding causing routing thrash, or routing failover amplifying load elsewhere).
4) Produces consistent customer-facing overload errors (see ADR-014).

This ADR defines **where circuit breakers and load shedding “live”** across the request path (Gateway → Routing → Runtime) and how signals flow.

sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Why am I seeing 503 if this is overload?”
sections.content:
“Why am I seeing 503 if this is overload?”

Approved response:
“503 is used when the platform is temporarily unable to serve the request due to load shedding or an open circuit breaker. It’s a deliberate, controlled response (with stable error codes) to prevent cascading failures and long tail latency.”

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Implementation notes (non-normative)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Implementation notes (non-normative)
sections.content:
Implementation notes (non-normative)

- Gateway admission should use a combination of:
  - token bucket (QPS) per tenant/route
  - concurrency caps for streaming endpoints
  - “regional overload state” multiplier for dynamic throttling (with hysteresis)
- Runtime should expose clear “reject reasons” that map into ADR-014 overload codes without leaking internals.
- Routing should mark fallback attempts and enforce max_attempts=1. Any further attempt must be a client retry honoring Retry-After.

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
- Total burst attempts: dominated by 2 tenants with scheduled batch jobs.
- Denial rate: ranged 0–18% by tenant depending on time-of-day; spikes correlated with telemetry lag and cooldown behavior.
- Admission controller p99: stable in us-east; spiky in eu-west (timeouts).
- Neighbor impact: one validated event (SUP-28455) where non-burst p99 regressed ~12–18% for ~20 minutes before mitigation.
- Billing reconciliation: identified retry double-counting bug; now fixed but we need ongoing automated checks.

What we changed during beta (already merged or in progress)

- Telemetry smoothing / prevent starvation under lag: GitHub:redwood/pr-23944
- Global circuit breaker for burst pools: GitHub:redwood/pr-23919
- SLO-based auto-gating (reduce/disable burst on non-burst regression): GitHub:redwood/pr-23988
- Billing idempotency + prevent double-counting: GitHub:redwood/pr-24108

GA readiness action items (must do)
P0 (blockers)
1) Telemetry freshness as a first-class signal

- Add metric + alert: “telemetry freshness seconds” by region/hardware + admission controller decision mode (fresh vs degraded).
- In degraded mode: enforce safer decisions (lower caps) + include explicit denial reason “TELEMETRY_STALE_DEGRADED_MODE”.
- Owner: Allison Grant + Logan Wright
- Target: by 2025-06-07

2) EU-West admission controller latency hardening

- Bound dependency calls with strict timeouts; add cached snapshots; add load shedding in controller.
- Define routing behavior when controller is slow: deterministic fallback decision + do not hammer controller.
- Owner: Jordan Lee + Mina Haddad
- Target: by 2025-06-10

3) Retry guidance + “Retry-After” semantics tied to reason codes

- Standardize: which denials are immediate (cap reached) vs transient (pool saturated) and include a backoff hint.
- Update docs + support macros.
- Owner: Peter Holtz + Kira Thompson
- Target: by 2025-06-12

4) Billing reconciliation automation

- Nightly job: compare metering export vs dashboard aggregates within tolerance; page billing on drift > X%.
- Owner: Nadia Rahman + Cole Summers
- Target: by 2025-06-12

P1 (strongly recommended for GA)
5) Cooldown redesign proposal

- Experiment with sustained-threshold cooldown vs proportional cooldown.
- Add simulation + real-world replay tests.
- Owner: Keiko Yamamoto
- Target: proposal by 2025-06-14; implement behind flag if time.

6) Neighbor impact circuit breaker thresholds

- Define concrete thresholds: p95 delta, tail amplification, and error rate deltas for non-burst tenants.
- Ensure breaker annotations show “why” and which tenant(s) triggered.
- Owner: Sean Gallagher
- Target: 2025-06-14

7) Priority tier fairness tests

- Extend multi-tenant integration tests to include tier mixes; assert starvation bounds.
- Owner: Jordan Lee
- Target: 2025-06-15

8) Console/config propagation SLO + fix

- Set expectation: config changes visible within N minutes; instrument end-to-end propagation time.
- Owner: Chloe Martin
- Target: 2025-06-15

Operational notes / runbook improvements

- Add a “first 5 minutes” checklist for burst-related pages:
  - Check global circuit breaker status
  - Check telemetry freshness + telemetry lag panels
  - Check admit/deny by reason code
  - Check pool saturation + queue depth
  - Check non-burst tenant latency deltas
  - Decide: tighten per-tenant cap vs disable region/hardware allow list
- Ensure runbook has a customer comms template (what happened, what we did, what to expect next).

1) Queue vs immediate denial for pool saturation

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
Burst Capacity Retro Notes

Source type: google_drive
Document ID: dsid_95c7aa5238f94570a8e0a8684736b666
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Dedicated Burst Capacity — Post-beta retro notes (SRE)
Doc goal
Capture what we learned from the Dedicated Burst Capacity beta (May 2025): what broke, which guardrails were too strict/too lax, what we changed during beta, and what must be completed before GA.

Retro logistics

- Date: 2025-05-28 (60 min)
- Facilitator: Rafael Mendes (SRE)
- Notetaker: Peter Holtz (Routing SRE)
- Beta window covered: 2025-05-06 to 2025-05-24
- Scope: burst pools (regional/hardware), admission controller, routing integration, SLO gates, dashboards/alerts, metering/billing hooks, supportability

Attendees (high signal contributors)

- SRE/Obs: Sean G., Rafael M., Peter H., Allison G., Sergio C.
- Infra/Fleet: Vanessa O., Keiko Y.
- Control plane/policy: Jordan L.
- Routing: Mina H.
- Billing/metering: Cole S., Nadia R.
- CS feedback: Rachel K.

What went well (keep)
1) Global safety cap + circuit breaker concept worked in practice

- We hit the cap once in staging and once “near miss” in prod beta; breaker prevented runaway neighbor impact.
- The playbook of “reduce caps -> drain queues -> disable burst for lowest tiers first” is operationally sound.

2) Denial reason codes improved triage materially

- Support/CS could distinguish “cap reached” vs “pool saturated” vs “cooldown” vs “telemetry stale”.
- Routing logs + reason codes made it clear where to look first.

3) Dashboards were mostly the right primitives

- Saturation, queue depth, admit/deny rates, and p95 deltas by tenant were enough to debug 80% of issues.
- SLO gate signal (non-burst tenant latency regression) is a good north star even if thresholds need tuning.

4) Rollout gating/feature flags prevented blast radius

- Per-region allow list + per-tenant enablement meant we could pause EU-West issues without impacting US-East.

What broke / painful incidents
A) Telemetry lag caused unfair denials + occasional starvation

- Symptom: a few tenants saw denial spikes while pool appeared underutilized; the “laggy” telemetry made the controller think they were still consuming burst tokens.
- Customer-visible effect: burst requests denied unexpectedly; some clients retried aggressively and amplified load.
- Root cause (likely): our admission controller relied on near-real-time usage signals; when signals were delayed, the smoothing window + token bucket refill behavior effectively penalized active tenants.
- Fix during beta: hotfix added smoothing + guard conditions + conservative fallback when telemetry freshness is below threshold.
- Ref: GitHub:redwood/pr-23944

B) EU-West burst admission timeouts (controller dependency chain)

- Symptom: admission calls intermittently timed out in eu-west under high request rate; routing fell back but increased gateway error rates briefly.
- Root cause: admission controller p99 latency spiked due to dependency (policy evaluation + fleet telemetry query) not being bounded; threadpool saturation.
- Mitigation: enable circuit breaker + temporarily tighten per-tenant caps + disable burst in eu-west allow list until patched.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28579

C) Billing: burst usage double-counted on retry paths

sections.section_path: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Summary
sections.heading: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Summary
sections.content:
Summary

On 2026-02-12, the production performance canary generated a burst of false-positive alerts across multiple models and regions shortly after enabling warning + paging rules in the first expansion beyond the initial 2-model rollout. Alerts were high volume (warning + paging) and repeatedly reopened due to dedupe failures, resulting in on-call interruption and a temporary release freeze request.

There was **no confirmed customer-facing latency regression** attributable to this incident. The event was an alerting/observability failure caused primarily by (1) **baseline drift + baseline key mismatch** and (2) **metric label cardinality inflation** that fragmented the canary’s time series, defeating min-sample gating and dedupe.

sections.section_path: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > Severity guidance (SRE)
sections.heading: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > Severity guidance (SRE)
sections.content:
Severity guidance (SRE)

Use the following guidelines when declaring severity:

- **SEV-1:** Widespread routing impact (many tenants), large latency/5xx increase, or rollout control plane causing sustained customer outage.
- **SEV-2:** Single large tenant impacted (SLA risk), or split mismatch causing repeated auto-pauses/rollbacks with user-visible degradation.
- **SEV-3:** Rollout stuck without service impact (customer blocked but production stable) or split mismatch limited to one region with low traffic.

If in doubt and customer-facing impact is ongoing, escalate severity early; mitigation (freeze/rollback) is typically low-risk.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Definitions
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Definitions
sections.content:
Definitions

- **Deployment**: A Dedicated inference endpoint identified by `deployment_id` and bound to a region and hardware pool.
- **Route**: A logical API capability within a deployment (e.g., `chat.completions`, `completions`, `embeddings`). For this SLO, throughput is evaluated at the **deployment level**, with route breakdowns used for diagnostics.
- **Committed Throughput Floor (CTF)**: The minimum throughput Redwood commits to sustain for a deployment under defined conditions. Expressed as **tokens/sec** (canonical) or **requests/sec** (only for non-tokenized routes; see below).
- **Observed Throughput**: Throughput computed from Redwood-side metering and timing, scoped to eligible requests.
- **SLO Window**: The evaluation interval used to determine compliance for a point in time (5 minutes).
- **Error Budget**: The allowed fraction of SLO windows that can be below the committed floor over the compliance period.

- Availability by tier (enterprise vs best-effort)

- queue depth and scheduler lag for backing pools

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
- Today we mostly deny quickly; some customers want queuing.
- SRE view: queuing can hide fleet pain and increase tail; if we add queueing it must be bounded with clear max wait + cancellation and must not break determinism.

2) How much “degraded mode” behavior is acceptable?

- If telemetry is stale, do we:
  a) deny all burst? (safe but may be overly strict)
  b) allow small burst with conservative cap? (better UX)
  c) continue as-is with risk? (not acceptable)
- Tentative: (b) with tight global caps + explicit surfaced state.

3) GA scope: region/hardware allow list

- Recommendation: GA in us-east H100 first; add eu-west after EU-West latency fix + game day rerun.

Appendix: customer support learnings (from tickets)

- SUP-28411 (unexpected denials): customers interpret “burst enabled” as “guaranteed extra capacity.” We must emphasize “best-effort within guardrails,” with clear reasons.
- SUP-28503 (429s): customers need explicit guidance on client-side backoff, concurrency control, and how to detect “you are at cap.”
- SUP-28488 (billing question): customers will audit the burst line item against their own job schedule; we need accurate exports + transparent calculation.

Next steps

- Rafael to turn P0s into a GA gate checklist and review in SRE staff meeting (2025-06-04).
- Schedule a short follow-up retro after GA week 1 to validate assumptions and update runbooks.

sections.section_path: Go Live Protocols Cross Org Communications Escalation 2027
sections.heading: Go Live Protocols Cross Org Communications Escalation 2027
sections.content:
| Level | Trigger example | Primary contact | Secondary contact | Action required |
|-------|-----------------|-----------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| L1 (CSM) | Customer questions, minor errors | CSM | SE | Acknowledge to customer within 15m, open internal thread |
| L2 (SRE) | Error rate >5% | Oncall SRE | SRE Lead | Execute diagnostics, apply mitigations (rate-limit, route switch) |
| L3 (SE/PM) | Persistent degradation >30m | Solutions Engineer | Product Manager | Coordinate config changes, model fallback, communicate to customer executives |
| L4 (Exec) | SLA breach or major incident | Head of Customer Success | Head of Engineering | Declare incident, engage legal/finance if SLA credits likely |

Note: The table above is intended as a quick reference. The full escalation paging list with phone numbers and PagerDuty IDs is stored in /confluence/people-ops/rosters and in the private channel pinned messages.

Common Mitigations (ordered by lowest customer impact first)
----------------------------------------------------------

- Increase routing to a higher-capacity pool (if Dedicated: burst pool)
- Apply tenant-level throttles to protect shared resources (quota reduce to 30% of projected steady-state)
- Enable model fallback: route to last-known-stable model snapshot
- Temporarily switch customer to hosted API endpoint (if allowed by contract)
- Quiesce long-running batch jobs from the customer side

Rollback and Safe-fail Strategies
--------------------------------

1. Safe rollback to previous routing config (SE executes):
   - Command: curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal.redwood/v1/route/revert -d '{"tenant":"<tenant-id>","to_config":"<previous-config-id>"}' 
   - Confirm routing table via: kubectl get svc ingress-<tenant> -o yaml (requires ops role)
2. Tenant quiesce API (customer-facing graceful shutdown):
   - POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/tenants/<tenant>/quiesce?actor=ops
   - Expected behavior: existing requests drain, new requests return 429 with Retry-After header.
3. Emergency switchback to hosted region: update DNS TTL and apply traffic policy TTL=30s for faster re-routing.

Communication Templates
-----------------------

- Customer-facing 1-line (acknowledge): "We are investigating increased latency for your production routes and will provide an update within 15 minutes. No action required from your side unless we ask."
- Customer-facing status update (10m cadence): include short bullet list: observed metric, action taken, owner, ETA for next update.
- Internal P0 page message sample:
  - "P0: <customer> production routes returning 503s since 08:12 UTC. Oncall SRE investigating. Initial hypothesis: ingress proxy thread exhaustion. Paging SRE Lead and SE. Next update in 5 minutes"

Telemetry checks / Queries (examples)
----------------------------------

- PromQL (errors): sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[5m])) > 0.05
- Token consumption anomaly (example):
  - Query: increase(token_count_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[30m]) / expected_token_rate > 2.0
- Synthetic validation command (curl):
  - curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -d '{"input":"synthetic health check"}' | jq '.latency_ms'

Post-Cutover (T+4 to T+72 hours)
--------------------------------

- Stability window monitoring: SRE to keep watch for 72 hours; escalate on any SLO breach.
- Cost and quota reconciliation: Finance Ops and CSM to review token consumption, forecast delta, and apply quota protections if needed.
- Customer QBR prep: collect first-week metrics and any incident notes for the 30-day QBR.

Runbook Ownership and RACI
-------------------------

sections.content:
SLOs (targets)

General notes

- SLOs are evaluated over a **rolling 28-day window**.
- Unless specified, targets apply per region (e.g., us-east, eu-west).
- We define both **p95 and p99** latency objectives for enterprise; best-effort uses p95 as primary.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Saturation requirement (practical interpretation)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Saturation requirement (practical interpretation)
sections.content:
Saturation requirement (practical interpretation)

This SLO is designed to answer: “When the customer is **trying** to use their Dedicated capacity, do we deliver the committed throughput?”

Therefore, compliance reporting only considers periods where the deployment is **meaningfully loaded**.

We define “meaningfully loaded” for a window as:

- `eligible_generation_wall_time_seconds >= 120` seconds within the 5-minute window

If a window does not meet the load threshold, it is treated as **insufficient demand** and excluded from compliance (removed from total). This prevents underutilized deployments from producing misleading ‘low throughput’ windows.

sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Computation > Fixed baseline artifact

Baseline Computation

Fixed baseline artifact

- Source: controlled perf-canary runs using the approved synthetic prompt distribution.
- For each baseline key, we store:
  - distribution summaries (p50/p95/p99) for each latency metric
  - mean and standard deviation where stable enough to be meaningful
  - tokens/sec distribution summaries
  - run metadata (time range, sample count, canary config version)
- Baseline validity: baseline is considered valid only if it meets minimum sample size requirements (see below) and passes sanity checks (no telemetry gaps, no error-rate spikes).

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.content:
What changed (customer-facing)

When the platform is saturated (GPU capacity, scheduler backlog, downstream dependency brownout), Redwood may reject requests *early* and predictably rather than allowing them to time out or generate random 5xx.

Customers may now see:

- **429** responses for admission / quota / per-tenant caps.
- **503** responses when a regional/model circuit breaker is open or the system is actively shedding load.

These responses:

- Include stable **error codes** and a machine-readable JSON payload.
- Typically include a **Retry-After** header to indicate safe retry timing.
- Include Redwood request/correlation IDs for tracing.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Positive
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Positive
sections.content:
Consequences

Positive

- Earlier, clearer shedding reduces tail latency and incident severity.
- Tenant/tier fairness is enforced consistently at the edge.
- Runtime remains protected even if gateway/routing misestimate load.
- Routing provides graceful degradation (fallback) without turning into a retry storm engine.

sections.section_path: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Context / problem
sections.heading: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Context / problem
sections.content:
Context / problem

Hosted canary rollouts require percentage-based traffic splitting on a Hosted route (e.g., 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%) while maintaining:

- Consistent cohorting so a given end user/conversation does not “flip” unpredictably
- Correctness under retries, streaming, and regional failover
- Clear metrics for baseline vs canary cohorts (including when the system must fall back)

Constraints:

- Data plane enforcement must be fast and operate without a central “assignment service.”
- Region routing and model fallback already exist; cohorting must compose cleanly.
- Customers may or may not provide stable end-user identifiers.

sections.section_path: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Initial support response (guidance provided)
sections.heading: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Initial support response (guidance provided)
sections.content:
Initial support response (guidance provided)

- Confirmed that the new system returns distinct reason codes and customers should key their retry/backoff behavior on:
  - "quota_exceeded" (respect quota windows; reduce steady-state rate)
  - "overload_protection_admission" (transient overload; respect Retry-After; use exponential backoff + jitter)
- Recommended changes:
  - Use exponential backoff with full jitter; cap concurrency; do not retry immediately.
  - Honor Retry-After; treat 429 as a signal to shed load client-side.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 1) Availability SLI (server success)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 1) Availability SLI (server success)
sections.content:
1) Availability SLI (server success)

**Definition:** percentage of requests that return an eligible success response.

- Success codes: `2xx` (and `3xx` if any internal redirects apply; typically none)
- Failures: `5xx`, `408`, `499` (client disconnect) are counted as failures unless explicitly excluded by route-specific rules below.

**Tier handling of 429:**

- **Enterprise:** `429` due to *overload shedding/admission control* counts as **unavailable** (because enterprise is protected; overload shed should be rare and indicates under-provisioning or misconfiguration).
- **Best-effort:** `429` due to overload shedding/admission control does **not** count as unavailable (it is expected behavior under pressure). Quota/rate-limit 429s are not counted as availability failures for either tier.

**Note:** 429 classification must be based on the reason code emitted by gateway/policy engine, not inferred from rate.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.content:
Alternatives considered

1) **Single global breaker at gateway only**

- Rejected: insufficient fidelity; cannot protect runtime safety in all cases; still allows deep queueing.

2) **Runtime-only backpressure (let everything in)**

- Rejected: overload manifests as queued latency/timeouts; poor customer semantics; wastes upstream work.

3) **Routing-driven global admission control**

- Rejected: routing is not the best place to enforce tenant fairness and local dependency breakers; risks complex control loops.

Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)

- GPU/node health signals indicate failures, evictions, ECC errors, or repeated container restarts.
- Saturation: GPU utilization pinned while throughput drops (suspected contention, thermal throttling, network bottleneck).
- Capacity: the deployment appears mapped to the wrong pool/shape or lacks the expected headroom.
- Region-wide capacity constraint impacting Dedicated pools.

Satellite Grove

Lead source: self-serve signup (product-led). Team: CTO (Aisha Kaur), Eng Lead (Mateo Lopez), PM (Rina Shah). Early discovery call 2026-03-02 via Fireflies ff-20260302-0934. Summary: building an in-app conversational assistant for their B2B workflow SaaS; must feel instant (streaming responses) and run on public cloud.

Key requirements:

- Streaming websocket support + chunked tokens (UX requires UI tokens arrive in <50ms increments).

sections.section_path: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Impact
sections.heading: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Impact
sections.content:
Impact

- Customer batch + online traffic intermittently fails with 429s, causing retry storms on their side.
- Reported elevated end-user latency due to retries; some requests fail after their max-retry budget.
- Customer concern: enterprise tier expected fewer 429s, not more.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > Latency SLOs by route and tier
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > Latency SLOs by route and tier
sections.content:
Latency SLOs by route and tier

Latency objectives are defined in terms of:

- **Chat streaming:** TTFB p95/p99
- **Non-streaming:** E2E p95/p99

| Route | Tier | Latency SLO (primary) | Latency SLO (secondary) | Measurement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | TTFB p95 ≤ 450ms | TTFB p99 ≤ 900ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Best-effort | TTFB p95 ≤ 900ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1800ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (non-streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 1.8s | E2E p99 ≤ 3.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 350ms | E2E p99 ≤ 800ms | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 700ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 550ms | E2E p99 ≤ 1.2s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 1.2s | (informational) p99 ≤ 2.5s | Gateway E2E |

**Notes / caveats**

- Latency SLOs assume nominal prompt and response sizes. Excessive prompt length or extreme max_tokens increases may be subject to policy limits; those requests are still included in latency metrics unless explicitly rejected by policy.
- Where fallback is permitted (route/model policy), latency SLI measures the actual served path; dashboards must annotate fallback activations.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.content:
Streaming-specific guidance

Streaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.

- Recommend **lower streaming concurrency** during peak periods.
- If the customer can tolerate it, recommend **shorter outputs** (reduce `max_tokens`) and/or **shorter prompts**.
- If a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.

response.query: What are the default size limits for file uploads and total request size for the new multipart upload support on the OpenAI-compatible API endpoints?

sections.section_path: Pr 18421 Multipart File Validation Limits
sections.heading: Pr 18421 Multipart File Validation Limits
sections.content:
Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout. Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compat error mapping and structured error shapes - [x] Tests: unit, integration, e2e - [x] Docs: compatibility notes and config guide - [x] Telemetry: counters for rejected parts and throttled requests - [x] Migration & rollout plan included Testing notes: the multipart parser uses a small constant memory footprint for each active part and yields part metadata to the handler; large parts trigger a streaming drain with early termination (413 response) to avoid OOM. Integration tests exercise combination of binary and text parts, wrong content-types, and boundary cases around the configured limits. Telemetry: added metrics api.multipart.rejected_content_type, api.multipart.rejected_size, api.multipart.accepted_parts and a hist for part sizes. Implementation details: - parser: runtime/multipart/stream_parser.py - validator: api/validation/multipart_validator.py - compat layer: api/openai_compat/input_adapter.py - config: config/defaults/multipart.yaml - docs: docs/openai-compat/multipart.md - tests: tests/unit/test_multipart_parser.py, tests/integration/test_openai_compat_multipart.py Error shape examples (structured output): when a part is rejected we return 413 with a JSON body {"error":{"type":"request_too_large","message":"part exceeds max_file_size","meta":{"part_name":"file","limit_bytes":10485760}}} and 400 for unsupported content-types with type unsupported_media_type. Observability: trace spans added around parse->validate->route dispatch to help pinpoint latency regressions. Related items: Linear ENG-2728 (multipart uploader stability), PM-146 (OpenAI compat feature parity).
Liam Chen: key question — do we need to special-case application/pdf? many partners send PDFs as application/pdf; current whitelist would block it. Suggest adding application/pdf or making whitelist configurable per-tenant.
Aisha Patel: replied — agreed, added application/pdf to tenant_whitelist in config and made default conservative. Added test case + note in docs explaining why binary blobs should be limited.

sections.section_path: Pr 18421 Multipart File Validation Limits
sections.heading: Pr 18421 Multipart File Validation Limits
sections.content:
Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout. Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compat error mapping and structured error shapes - [x] Tests: unit, integration, e2e - [x] Docs: compatibility notes and config guide - [x] Telemetry: counters for rejected parts and throttled requests - [x] Migration & rollout plan included Testing notes: the multipart parser uses a small constant memory footprint for each active part and yields part metadata to the handler; large parts trigger a streaming drain with early termination (413 response) to avoid OOM. Integration tests exercise combination of binary and text parts, wrong content-types, and boundary cases around the configured limits. Telemetry: added metrics api.multipart.rejected_content_type, api.multipart.rejected_size, api.multipart.accepted_parts and a hist for part sizes. Implementation details: - parser: runtime/multipart/stream_parser.py - validator: api/validation/multipart_validator.py - compat layer: api/openai_compat/input_adapter.py - config: config/defaults/multipart.yaml - docs: docs/openai-compat/multipart.md - tests: tests/unit/test_multipart_parser.py, tests/integration/test_openai_compat_multipart.py Error shape examples (structured output): when a part is rejected we return 413 with a JSON body {"error":{"type":"request_too_large","message":"part exceeds max_file_size","meta":{"part_name":"file","limit_bytes":10485760}}} and 400 for unsupported content-types with type unsupported_media_type. Observability: trace spans added around parse->validate->route dispatch to help pinpoint latency regressions. Related items: Linear ENG-2728 (multipart uploader stability), PM-146 (OpenAI compat feature parity).
Liam Chen: key question — do we need to special-case application/pdf? many partners send PDFs as application/pdf; current whitelist would block it. Suggest adding application/pdf or making whitelist configurable per-tenant.
Aisha Patel: replied — agreed, added application/pdf to tenant_whitelist in config and made default conservative. Added test case + note in docs explaining why binary blobs should be limited.

Ravi Singh: please ensure the validator surfaces clear errors for multipart boundary parsing failures; I saw a flaky crash in an initial run.
Aisha Patel: replied — parser now catches malformed boundary exceptions and returns a 400 with error.type=malformed_multipart and includes low-signal debug id for tracing; updated tests.
Sofia Alvarez: approved — addressed my comments about metrics naming and added a suggestion to include counter tags for tenant_id and route_id.
CI Bot: integration-tests failed on first run due to test harness timeout; rerun completed successfully.
QA: noted an edge case where client SDK retries might double-submit large files; added a recommendation in docs and an optional idempotency header support in adapter.
Added multipart/form-data support on OpenAI-compat API paths with strict content-type validation and configurable per-file and per-request size limits. Default limits: 10MiB per file, 50MiB per request. Feature is behind a feature flag and can be enabled per-tenant. See docs/openai-compat/multipart.md for migration steps.
